(The Subject: The Tantra) Oṃ. May there be well-being. Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa. Oṃ. Salutations to the illustrious Rāma. Oṃ. There was a most excellent divine sage named Agastya who, once upon a time, went to the hermitage of Sutīkṣṇa in the Daṇḍaka forest on the banks of the Gautamī.

The sage Sutīkṣṇa approached him with devotion and performed the rites of hospitality for that knower of Brahman, offering perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, water, and the respectful offerings of water for the feet and the guest-offering (*arghya*). Sutīkṣṇa [said] to that muni... [text continues]

Having prostrated before him as he sat comfortably, he said: "O treasure of asceticism, my life has become fruitful simply by your illustrious arrival. Today, through thousands of births, my desired fruit of penance bears fruit. O Sage, I have been constantly tormented by desire, anger, and other passions; though I performed sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees, I did not see [the truth] correctly. O best of sages, though I gave all gifts to worthy recipients and performed difficult austerities to cross the ocean of existence, what shall I do now, father? Tell me, where shall I go? Thus addressed, he spoke to him:

Free from desire for the vessel-born sage (Agastya), that bull among sages reflected for a moment upon the sequence of past and future events. Agastya said: "O Bull-bannered One, I shall tell you the entire secret, by which conviction the Knower of Self previously attained [liberation] through the grace of Pārvatī. The Lord said: "Corrupted by defects such as lust and anger, they are born again and again there, and likewise, being deluded, they dissolve again. Transmigrating beings are cooked in the Raurava and other hells; then, due to the remnants of their karma, they are born on earth as the lame, the blind, the deaf, and so forth. [The text continues: "Having performed [deeds]..."

Having become insects and the like, those wandering again in this world on earth are afflicted by leprosy and other diseases; some are slain by thieves, tigers, and the like; they enter water or fire, or wander from country to country at the command [of fate].

Those who steal the wives and wealth of others constantly torment the virtuous; those who live daily upon the property of gods and Brahmins, those who are *rājasa* and *tāmasa*, those who are destroyers, those who live as forest-dwellers, and those joined with sons, wives, and so forth—alas, they whirl in a vortex of suffering. At the onset of the Kali age, all are likewise *rājasa* and *tāmasa*, practicing what is forbidden.

We do not delude many others; rather, as the Lord is in this world, so too are His servants. Therefore, all my followers—whether in acts of harm or in what is pleasing, whether in subjugation, attraction, inciting enmity, paralyzing, or expulsion—become partakers of the fruits by constantly propitiating us both. O Goddess of the gods, those who, disregarding the dharma appropriate to their caste and stage of life, offer us flesh, blood, or wine, become ghosts, spirits, piśācas, and brahmarākṣasas. Furthermore, their...

The Brahmins who are entitled to the Vedas are born as *tejāyan* (radiant ones); they are not born with that [universal] form, but rather in accordance with their own respective defects. Pārvatī said: "O Lord of Gods, this dharma does not bring benefit to others. Therefore, O Lord of Gods, tell me that dharma which is dear to the Treasure of Compassion. Īśvara said: "O Goddess, I shall speak the truth regarding what you ask me. I am the *Haṃsa* (the Supreme Soul) of all worlds; therefore, the *Haṃsī* (the Supreme Consciousness) is my beloved. Those beings who destroy [evil] by both lawful and unlawful means, and who offer [their actions] unto all beings—they are dear to me."
O Sadāpriye, I always destroy the darkness of egoism; O Bhāvini, I constantly slay living beings. Since the destruction of my own karma is achieved thereby, violence itself is dear to me.

O beloved of my beloved, all those who act according to my will perform service in accordance with their station as masters of the worlds. O Queen of the Gods, those who offer even their own flesh and blood to me with devotion produce great joy for me. Likewise, those who, according to the prescribed rites, provide flesh and blood for my followers also bring us satisfaction.

"Brahmā creates beings; Viṣṇu protects them; I, however, destroy those very beings—such is our respective nature. Brahmā abides in the quality of *rajas*, Viṣṇu abides in the quality of *sattva*, and I am the abode of the quality of *tamas*. We each perform such actions according to our own duties, in accordance with those respective qualities. O Goddess, this crossing of the ocean of worldly existence is extremely difficult for those who are harmful and whose minds are seized by desire and other passions; tell me, O beloved, how can there be liberation for them? (39) Thus ends [the section] in the *Śrī Agastisaṃhitā*.

[First Chapter] (1) Pārvatī said: "O Lord, what must one worship to obtain liberation through action or non-action? For one desiring release, the destruction of worldly existence—which makes rebirth difficult—is hard to attain. Īśvara said: "Listen, O highly fortunate Goddess; I shall tell you a secret, knowing which a living being is released from the bondage of birth and saṃsāra. Without hands or feet, he is swift; though holding, he is not grasped; though seeing, he is unseen. Without ears, he indeed hears. He is the supreme light, sound, and form. He knows that which is to be known; he is the omniscient one who is unknowable even by the all-knowing. He is the Lord who is to be known. He is the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa) among men, and the woman among women."

The Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who is devoid of the characteristics of gender—free from the forms of female, male, and neuter—is the Lord of all, the embodiment of all, Hari, who consists of all the gods. He is composed of truth and knowledge, infinite, without beginning, whose very form is bliss. He is unborn; by mere remembrance of Him, the afflictions of birth and so forth are destroyed. His meditation is the means for all beings, yet it leads to non-return [to worldly existence]. That Lord must be meditated upon by those of all social classes (varṇas) according to the rules prescribed for their respective stages of life (āśrama), for the destruction of saṃsāra, and then one does not return again. Those who, abandoning what is prescribed for their own stage of life, worship Him in that form [alone], [attain the goal].

Indeed, one is not liberated from the bondage of worldly existence merely by following whatever rules are prescribed for whichever stage of life (*āśrama*) in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Purāṇas*; rather, those seeking liberation must not abandon their specific duty.

Therefore, adhering to one's own rule, one should practice meditation with an undistracted mind. O Beloved, the wise man perceives this entire universe of moving and non-moving beings as being like the cognition of a dream—unreal, because it is an object of sight, just like a mirage. Apart from the nature of pure consciousness, he sees that which is distinct from himself as being projected by the Self through the form of the Seer. This world, which appears separate from the Self that is Truth and Bliss, is [seen] by him who is alone, whose mind and self are absorbed in That.

One should contemplate that with undistracted mind, thinking "I am That," by means of the self regarding the self. This world, imagined through one's own ignorance, appears as something distinct from oneself; yet since one imagines it by means of oneself alone, O Goddess, it is not ultimately real, even if one imagines it to be so. For what difference could there be between a hair-tip and a mountain when viewed with the eye of reality? The ancient path has been traversed by the ancients, those knowers of the supreme self; they have declared that the words beyond speech are remembered as the Supreme. Among the pure lineages of those starting from Brahmā, within the noble families of mothers and fathers, women are not unchaste, nor are men [unfaithful].

O Goddess, the sacrifices serve the student of the Vedas, and they are honored individually by every person. Wherever there is a lineage of teachers and disciples, even when one falters during sleep, that very discipline constitutes an āśrama among those who possess it, even at times when it might seem to cease. At those times, gifts are bestowed upon seekers; in all those lineages, one should manifest the Brahman through the primary and secondary instructions of the teacher to those who know Brahman. O Goddess, the Supreme Brahman is itself nothing other than this; all this is indeed Brahman.

Truth, truth indeed is being revealed: after thousands of millions of births, some rare person whose sins have been washed away, having attained self-restraint, perceives it directly. The state of being whose sole form is true knowledge and the tasting of the nectar-essence of bliss is experienced by the wise man himself through his own good fortune. Oh, what great merit! Oh, what great dharma! O beloved, there is nothing higher than this; even when all other rites have not been performed, this is the supreme expiation. [Thus ends the second chapter of the Śrī Agasti Saṃhitā. Pārvatī said:

"O All-Knowing One, Lord of all worlds, Destroyer of all suffering, O Treasure of Compassion, tell me the path that is easy for everyone to traverse. The Lord said: "Listen attentively, O Goddess, to how this is attained. He who is the Lord of all, who consists of all, and who is devoted to the welfare of all beings, has assumed a formless body for the sake of helping everyone. Being affectionate toward his devotees, he acts spontaneously in the world; like a god, he experiences both suffering and happiness according to the nature of his devotees. Whenever fear arises among living beings, at that time, he destroys that very fear."

He who perceives the ultimate reality manifested Himself more abundantly through forms such as the fish, the tortoise, and the boar; appearing at various times, He, who is affectionate toward His devotees, removed the suffering of all beings, including the *dhū* castes, the stages of life (*āśramas*), and His devotees. Though formless, the benefactor assumes those very forms. This unborn, infinite, and peaceful one, the creator of all beings, has descended at times out of compassion for His devotees. O Lord of the gods, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa appeared on earth from the Ocean of Milk along with Śeṣa, bearing the conch and the discus.

In the Tretā Yuga, Nārāyaṇa appeared as the son of Daśaratha together with the gods, beginning with Brahmā; Śeṣa became Lakṣmaṇa, Lakṣmī became Jānakī, and the conch and discus were born as Bharata and Śatrughna. All the gods likewise became monkeys. Thus, for the sake of pacifying the fear of the gods and sages, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, renowned as Śrī Rāma, descended to the earth for the benefit of all the worlds. Some, desiring to behold him directly while he was performing penance, sat amidst five fires during the summer and lay upon the bare ground during the rainy season.

In this way, some endured [their penance] in waters that were as cold as ice; others wandered for alms, observing the rules of fasting and breaking their fasts; still others withered their bodies through the practice of *kṛcchra* penances, while some passed their time according to the *cāndrāyaṇa* rite. Others, consuming only vegetables, brought their bodies to exhaustion—oh, how remarkable! Here, some who eat only at night or subsist on leaves dwell in forests difficult to traverse, contemplating the eternal Truth within their hearts. With undistracted minds, they constantly recite the names of the senses and their lineages, chanting "Victory to Rāma! and "O Rāma! aloud.

Some, having dissolved their minds into the abode of the Self and become immortal, remain in a state of bliss; others, facing my western direction, meditate for a long time upon the Supreme Goddess in that most excellent temple, as if they were wise ones who had already attained Him.
Some, devoted to His service, dwell within the very palaces; others, wishing to see those who despise them and to dispute with them like kinsmen, [remain there].

Others, for the purpose of teaching sciences and even for the sake of combat, [stay there]. Some, becoming enemies of the Discus-wielder (Viṣṇu), exerted themselves among those He detested; others, subsisting on a diet of milk, dwelt right upon the shores of the ocean.

O hero with restless eyes, the penance of some cannot even be remembered; what will this Lord do upon seeing such a most terrible sound? Out of compassion for the ascetics performing penance here, He who is affectionate toward His devotees assumes a human form for all His devotees. O Lord of Gods, by mere meditation, He destroys great sins; by chanting and remembering Him, He wards off ten million murders. Even those sinners who say "Rāma, Rāma, Rāma," He delivers them from thousands of crores of sins—this is not otherwise.

Through their fierce austerity, that treasure-house of compassion became manifest to them; for by the merit of all those yogis, He was perceived directly by all, even beyond what can be expressed by the words and minds of practitioners.

Oh, by the excellence of his fortune, this man, while conducting his worldly affairs, bestows the fruit of penance and grants both prosperity and knowledge through his asceticism. O fortunate one, there is nothing difficult to attain for embodied beings through austerity.
Although the All-pervading Lord has already attained all desires within the range of His own mind, He assumes a human form upon the earth and rejoices like a mortal. Oh, how great is His mercy!

Indeed, everything is attained through renunciation; even in this regard, O lady with the gait of an elephant, what could be greater than this gain? For one whose wealth is penance, whose fortune is penance, and for whom penance grants success everywhere—even servitude to ascetics is difficult to obtain, O Goddess. [Thus ends the third chapter of the Śrī Agastisaṃhitā. Pārvatī said:

O Lord of Devas, how is it that all have attained devotion by worshipping Him whose sole characteristic is the bliss of the pair of feet worshipped by the lords of yogis? Tell me this, if You have compassion for me.

The Lord said: O sinless one, listen to the secret conclusion of Hiraṇyagarbha, by knowing which one is liberated from delusion, misfortune, and the accumulation of diseases. O blessed lady, I shall impart that to you, so that you may grasp its essence. Formerly, Brahmā performed penance for three hundred crores of kalpas along with many lords of sages, observing a difficult vow of fasting.

Standing in the midst of fires, intent upon his worship, he propitiated [the Lord] with excessive devotion through continuous rites of adoration and the like. After a long time, even the God of gods became manifest before him. Furthermore—

Due to the abundance of merit of all of them and his own beloved [devotee], the Lord appeared before them—dark as a fresh blue cloud, adorned with all ornaments, graced with a crown of matted hair and bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; beautified by a tiara, necklaces, armlets, and jeweled earrings; clothed in a pair of yellow garments resembling refined gold; consisting of pure light, such that ten million suns, moons, lightning flashes, meteors, and fires seemed to merge and become one. At that moment, Brahmā stood transfixed for an instant, rendered motionless and bewildered, and the sage offered praise.

Having bowed down again and again along with his kinsmen, he thought: "I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose, and I have attained my goal through these relatives; the Blessed One is well-pleased here, and my life has become fruitful.

Reflecting thus, "How shall I please the God?", he worshipped the Lord and praised Him with the Rig, Yajur, and Sama Vedas, with many scriptures out of reverence, and with all the works of Manu and others intent upon establishing Dharma. Being further gratified by the sages, he said: "You alone are called the one whose eyes are on all sides, whose faces are on all sides; being the one, You are likewise the one whose arms and feet are on all sides."

Creating the worlds of Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, you are the ruler of all; with your eyes, your arms, your actions, your feet, and even your nostrils, you behold everything everywhere. You concentrate, you hear, and you go about this entire world, O doer of all. You smell, yet nothing here remains unknown to you, O Lord. You alone are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; you are indeed Keśava. You are the Puruṣa of a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet. You are the form of earth, water, and fire, as well as of wind and space. You are the effect, the agent, and the creator.

"O sole cause of the three worlds, subtler than the subtle, greater than the great, you yourself are the center within the center; you are free from all conceptual constructs. O Lord, he who follows you [is blessed].

Pleased by these and many other such Vedic hymns of praise, Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, spoke thus to Brahmā out of compassion: "O Brahmā, I am pleased with you because of your fierce penance. Choose whatever you desire; O lotus-born one, I shall grant it to you. Thus addressed by the powerful Viṣṇu, he replied: "If you are indeed pleased, O Lord of Gods..."

O God of gods, if you have compassion for me, O Mother, you will accept my desired service. I am deeply distressed by misfortune and the suffering of poverty. O Lord of gods, it appears to me that all this is exactly so for us. What shall I do, O Lord of gods? Tell me, O Supreme Person; all my subjects are corrupted by defects such as lust and anger, and due to their past karma, not one remains who is free from them. What means is there for human beings who are devoted, O you who are kind to your devotees? [This state continues] until the fall of this body, but beyond that—no further.

For the sake of accomplishing his purpose, the God of gods spoke thus for the attainment of enjoyment and liberation: "Having reflected a little, out of compassion, he imparted the six-syllabled mantra (*ṣaḍakṣara*). He bestowed the arrangement of each individual syllable, the sequence, the six limbs (*aṅga*), the ritual procedure, the yantra, and the letters of the mantra. Even the God of gods communicated this secret to him in private. By the mere acquisition of that, at that very moment, its fruit was attained: he became the sovereign of all and even then possessed omniscience. Furthermore, whatever lordship he desired also came to pass."

"By the grace of the Lord of All and by penance, what cannot be obtained even by all the sages? Then, by His command, Brahmā [bestowed] all those [powers] along with their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and locations. Thereupon Viṣṇu said to Him: 'O Brahmā, you shall be the seer (*ṛṣi*) of this mantra; you are the knower of all mantras. I am Rāma, the deity; Gāyatrī is the supreme meter among meters. *Māṃ* (ma) and *tāṃ* (taṃ) shall be the seed-syllable (*bīja*), granting the primordial fruit. *Namaḥ* is designated as the power (*śakti*); the leader of the mantra ends in *namaḥ*. O Brahmā, placing *rāmāya* in the middle, one should offer everything to Him. In this world, there is enjoyment (*bhukti*...')"

"Liberation shall occur at the end of the body, and whatever else may be desired shall arise through my grace. With focused mind and no other thought, you must perform this continuously with devotion for a long time.

With your heart fixed on me, worship me alone for a long time; meditating on me alone with your mind, you shall come to me and not otherwise. Expand this very Sūtra and teach it in detail to your disciples. Having spoken thus, the lotus-eyed Lord vanished right there. And the venerable Prajāpati, together with the sages, performed the rites according to the injunctions every day.
Then Brahmā, having placed the command upon their heads, became the teacher for all of them; "O noble ones, by this very [command] of yours, everything desired shall come to pass. (40)

[Thus ends the fourth chapter in the glorious Agasti-saṃhitā. (4) Sutīkṣṇa said: O knower of the ancient Purāṇas, O best among those who know the meaning of all branches of knowledge, O foremost of Brahmins, what did Agastya do after that? In what form did the Lord then enlighten her? Agastya said: Then, fixing Rāma within her heart, that lotus-eyed one, devoted to no other, resolved upon liberation. After hearing the secret essence of the Siddhānta of Hiraṇyagarbha, she was overcome by desire and the like.

Then the Lord quickly turned back toward that beloved one who was established in pure knowledge alone. Having understood her desire for the cessation of worldly existence, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign who grants all desires, spoke to her: "O Noble One, you are Mūlaprakṛti (Root Nature), and I am the eternal Puruṣa. You are the cause of the world's origin; therefore, perform the contemplation of that Truth. If there were to be a cessation of this [world], what would be beneficial for you? O Auspicious One, there is nothing equal to me, nor is there anything higher than me. For the effect is not separate from the cause."
"Tell us, O Bhava, where shall we go? For a hundred kalpas, the gods will come into being through your grace;

this entire world shall never exist [as it is now]. While you dwell thus, O Goddess, why do you intend to abandon everything? It is not at all fitting for you, O Goddess, to renounce anything now. Thus addressed, the goddess with eyes like blue lotus petals spoke to the Lord: "O Lord, my life-breath is yours; what must I do? She said: "This virtuous latent impression (*sadvāsanā*) has not yet arisen within me, O Master. At some time...

"O Pārvatī, accept my state as your husband. Thus addressed, he spoke again to that daughter of the Himavat: "O Goddess, for the sake of worshipping Śrī Rāma, perform his worship every day with the necessary materials;
do not act otherwise, O beloved. By this alone, no fear whatsoever shall arise here or in the hereafter. In the Kali age, the entire flood of sins is destroyed by mere chanting (*saṃkīrtana*).

What need is there to speak of worship performed with devotion using perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings? O beloved, everything that is even mentally conceived comes to pass through such worship alone."

Otherwise, one does not attain auspiciousness in this world or the next merely by possessing knowledge, even as much as the moon, without giving gifts such as gold and the like. O lady of noble lineage, if a householder were not to give gifts, nor offer oblations, nor worship according to the prescribed rites, who indeed would perform these daily? There is no authority for a student (*brahmacārī*) to give; for whom, then, among all the teachers here, would one give what is desired? Forest-dwellers have no capacity [for such acts], and they do not exist in this Kali age. A wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*) [attains his goal] through knowledge alone; [for him] there are no gifts or fire-oblations.

Without these, one is not liberated from the demons of all suffering; it is not otherwise. O lotus-faced one, both the unrenounced wandering mendicant and the renounced householder shall sink into the *Kumbhīpāka* hell. Therefore, virtuous women who are householders and seekers of auspiciousness should offer gifts, abundant worship, and honors with articles for adoration—using sandalwood, agallochum, musk, camphor, and snow-white moon-pearls; with ablutions of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), with red lotuses, with many flower garlands, and with *dūrvā* grass and *akṣa* beads.

Together with them, they should diligently worship with blue lotuses (*nīlotpala*), jasmine (*mallikā*), *karavīra*, and *campaka* flowers; with *jātī*, *prasūta*, and *bilva*; and also with *puṃnāga*, *bakula*, plantain (*kadalī*), and *ketakī* blossoms; with *vāruṇa*, *aśoka*, and *kiṃśuka*; and with fragrant, captivating flowers such as *nāgara* and others—both those that are sharp and those that are soft—as well as with sprouts and leaves produced in water or on land. In this manner, they should daily and with great effort properly prepare many other such flowers according to their ability, making it most excellent.

For the attainment of their desired goals, they should worship [the deity] three times a day or once a day, day and night, with great reverence and various kinds of flour-based offerings cooked in milk, water, or ghee—such as *phenā*, *apūpa*, and *vaṭa* cakes;
with curd-rice, sweetened water, soups, and various side dishes; and with an extensive variety of items including *vaṭī*, *vaṭa*, and *upaśoka*.

They should worship day and night with *ārārtika* lamps, incense, and lights arranged in sixfold cycles, with many rows of lamps, and with *kaṅkola*, cardamom, betel nuts, nutmegs, and camphor powder.

With betel leaves that are well-scented and accompanied by betel-nut, one should perform the worship of Mahādeva daily with devotion for the sake of [attaining] the desired goal. Having prepared everything with effort according to one's own capacity, O fair-faced one, this is the rule for householders and not for others. Those seeking auspiciousness should give gifts and offer oblations into the consecrated fire; O beautiful lady, they should perform these rites daily with the thought of offering everything to Rāma.

Thus, having followed the rules for householders as well as those for celibate students without transgression, if they should perform these diligently according to their respective capacities, [the goal will be attained].

Through worship and its means, all prosperity is attained here; even that which is difficult for those gods to obtain is within reach, O auspicious one, if you desire welfare—provided it is pure and possible. As long as life lasts, if you worship Rāma according to the rules, by this alone, O lady of excellent hips, you shall always possess welfare. Likewise, virtuous women, householders, and even celibate students, having propitiated Rāma along with his retinue using the aforementioned means, should worship him day and night with whatever they can afford. For them, both worldly enjoyment and liberation will surely come to pass.

Or otherwise, if forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*) were to act in this manner every day, they would not turn back from *saṃsāra* due to the fault of transgressing their vows; for they would become those who have fallen after having ascended, and would be partakers of suffering. Non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is the supreme duty for them, and this is their path: indeed, those various [objects] are not obtained apart from non-violence. They are worshipped only through means of worship fashioned within the self, not externally; for you, O Yogis, external [worship] is not praised for them. This is practiced by those whose intellect is fixed on the Vedic meters (*chandodhiyas*) in many forms; meditation (*dhyāna*) also—

Because it bestows the fruit of the desired object—whether worship, auspiciousness, or prosperity—one should contemplate the Self within the mind of reality; yet one should not again turn back from contemplating the Self as being identical with both. O Rāma, those who always perceive themselves as such and sport [in that state], for them there is no suffering whatsoever, nor any calamities arising from evil deeds. [The venerable Agastya said: "O Śrī, the greatness of Tulasī has been remembered in some places. Agastya said: "Listen, I shall diligently declare the majesty of Tulasī. Formerly, having performed fierce penance, that ascetic woman made a vow: 'May Tulasī be more beloved than all other flowers and leaves to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the three worlds, just as the daughter of Janaka was dear to Rāma; likewise, may Tulasī be the sole purifier of all the worlds. He who worships Rāma every day with even a single leaf of Tulasī goes to the eternal Brahman, from which return is difficult to attain."

If one worships Hari every day with a thousand blue lotuses, that same fruit is obtained only after a thousand years. Among all flowers, the lotus is declared the best; among those flowers, a garland made of them becomes a hundred-thousand-fold or ten-million-fold more meritorious. A single leaf of sacred Tulasī placed upon the head of Viṣṇu, O wise one, bestows infinite fruit when accompanied by the recitation of mantras. One should offer a garland fashioned from Tulasī leaves—interspersed with other flowers, anointed with sandalwood paste—upon the head of Śrī Rāma. What need is there for more?

What is the use of many sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), or of visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*), or of gifts, or even of severe austerity? One who, having restrained their speech and fixed the mind upon Viṣṇu, worships [Him] with garlands of *tulasī*, shall obtain the fruit of ten million sacrifices. For those submerged in the well of the ocean of worldly existence, this is the goad that pulls them out. Leaves, flowers, and fruits of the glorious *tulasī* when offered to Rāma illuminate the path to liberation and grant all perfections (*siddhi*). One should offer garlands interspersed with other flowers; indeed, all [the merit] of the *tulasī*...

O ascetic, the grove of Tulasī has been fashioned there; it shines, surrounded by hundreds of flowers and leaves from within that garden. There, Rāghava himself, together with Sītā, personally offers [the offerings] out of devotion to him. Having surrounded the thorny Tulasī leaf with a forest-like enclosure, O Lord of Gods, nothing else is more worthy of worship than that. Those who drink the water from the Sālagrāma stone, which is perfumed by Tulasī leaves, for them no other drink is equal. It is like the water of the Gaṅgā itself, O God.

Among all flowers, the *tulasī* leaf is praised as the supreme lotus; by worshipping Rāma with devotion and according to the rules using sacred *tulasī* leaves, one is liberated from the crocodile of suffering throughout thousands of future births. O ascetic, for those of any caste, stage of life, or otherwise, worship of Him is the sole means; He grants all desired objects. One should worship Hari with whatever leaves, petals, or flowers are fit for worship. Alas, even the deficiencies and excesses of one's past actions reach fruition [as merit], and for such a person, there is no suffering in hell.
Whether one is most sinful or even sinless, it is the truth, the absolute truth, there is no doubt, that he who worships Rāma with Tulasī leaves mixed with the water of the Gaṅgā—

placing [the water] upon his head while reciting the mantra and sprinkling it— while closing his eyes, the wise man fixing Rāma within his heart, and performing this practice either repeatedly or even once, becomes meditated upon by all for the sake of my own liberation. Even if one has no true gurus and no formal sequence of initiation, if they speak the Rāmarakṣā and offer a Tulasī leaf...

Yet, even by a hundred other initiations (*dīkṣā*), that fruit is not obtained. Among all those who have been initiated, Rāma-dīkṣita is the most excellent. Neither a guru, nor time, nor the worship of other deities is required; only the worship of Rāma accompanied by *tulasī* leaves is required. If one worships Hari while wearing the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*) and *tulasī* garlands, whatever he does will yield infinite fruit. Even if the means for his complete propitiation should be deficient, it is said that it is fulfilled by a mere *tulasī* leaf alone. [Regarding] Śālagrāma...

O ascetic, even Hari himself is not able to fully describe in a single lifetime the greatness of Maśilā, the Gaṅgā, and Tulasī. This [Tulasī] destroys worldly existence and bestows all desired objects;

there exists nothing else on earth more purifying than this. He who diligently fashions a rosary from Tulasī wood becomes the personified form of the syllable-garland (the alphabet), and his merit becomes inexhaustible. Whatever camphor, agallochum, musk, or sandalwood one might rub upon the head of Rāma is not equal to the mere touch of Tulasī wood. Even the forest of Tulasī [is supreme].
An area extending for one *krośa* all around becomes a place of purification, just like the current of the Gaṅgā. By seeing and touching Tulasī when it has been planted and watered, one is purified.

When worshipped with diligence, she bestows the fruits of all desires. She is indeed honored by all four castes (*varṇas*) and especially by those in the various stages of life (*āśramas*), as well as by women and men;
she grants what is desired. Those who constantly perform circumambulation and offer salutations—no trace of their misdeeds is seen here, for they have attained a vision of no other.

O ascetic, those who behold this do not suffer affliction in hell; they proceed to the supreme state. Whether it be what ought to be done or what ought not to be done, whether deficient or even excessive, one should take a leaf of *tulasī*, meditate upon Rāma, and offer it. Saying "Salutation to Rāma," then "Salutation to Acyuta," and thereafter "Salutation to Ananta"—one should utter these words beginning with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) just once in the presence of the *tulasī*, O Sage; thus it becomes fruitful. [Thus ends the sixth chapter of the Śrī Agastisaṃhitā. (6)

Sutīkṣṇa said: "O best of sages, tell me everything regarding the greatness of Rāma’s King of Mantras (*mantrarāja*), which was previously spoken by Brahmā. Agastya said: "I shall relate all of that to you, exactly as it was told by Brahmā in the presence of Purāri (Śiva) in the past; listen with focused attention to me. There is a city named Vārāṇasī, which captivates the mind of Śiva;
Śiva always dwells there together with Pārvatī. All his worshippers, desiring liberation, have approached him with devotion, having renounced everything."

Remaining right there, constantly uttering "Sadāśiva, Śiva," devoted solely to Śiva, with their mind, body, and speech dedicated to Śiva, and intent upon Śiva—Śiva beheld them repeatedly and became overwhelmed with anxiety, deeply distressed as he wondered, "How shall I grant liberation to these? With his mind and body dedicated to Śiva, he remained right there along with the Gaṇas, sages, gods, and demons. Then the Grandfather (Brahmā) arrived at the earthly realm (Bhūrloka), which was thus purified; and upon seeing him, the Lord (Śiva) acted with great agitation.
He reported that which was highly esteemed and beneficial. Then the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, said to the Grandfather: "O Brahmā, is it well with you? You have come here after a long time.

By your illustrious arrival, even though I am worshipped by devotees and honored by the worlds, I am truly gratified. Tell me, by what means shall I grant them that fruit for which seekers of liberation pray until final release? Thus addressed by the Lord, Druhiṇa spoke: "O Best of the Raghus, there exists a means to be imparted; he has granted it to me."

"O Maheśvara, having performed penance for a long time, I have finally attained that Supreme One; there is no other protector known to me besides Him. Rāma will surely show grace toward me; of this there is no doubt. The Lord said: "If you have compassion for me, what do you wish to say further? Being thus addressed by Him, Dadhīci asked, "Where and when shall I be joined with Him? [Śiva replied:

"At the holy ford of the Gaṅgā, at Lolārka, on the occasion of a solar eclipse, He will grant him the supreme mantra, the six-syllabled King of Mantras. Restrained in mind, he went to that very place where the Bull-bannered Lord resided.

For a hundred *manvantaras*, through devotion, meditation, fire-offerings, worship, and other rites, the Lord Śrī Rāma became pleased and said to Śaṅkara: "Choose whatever you desire, even if it be difficult for the gods to attain; I shall grant that very thing to you, O bull-bannered one. Then, with supreme joy toward Viṣṇu, the Lord said to him: "By the mere sight of you, I am blessed and my purpose is fulfilled. All these followers of mine worship me as the Supreme for the sake of liberation; therefore, act for their benefit—that alone is my own desire."

"Is there anything else more supreme than that which I might desire? Thus, at that very time and in that very place, those who were his worshippers, consisting entirely of light, attained dissolution into Viṣṇu alone. Then I spoke again: "O Lord, when you are pleased, speak what is desired; I shall grant it, even if it be a request difficult to obtain. Being thus addressed, he, the benefactor and lover of his devotees, spoke again for the benefit of all the worlds: "O Lord, those who, whether by their own accord or through another, wherever it may be, renounce their lives..."

"O Lord, for those who die anywhere—whether on the banks of the Gaṅgā, on its shore, or elsewhere—their fruit shall be liberation; there is no other end to it. Śrī Rāma said: "O Lord of Gods, let even worms, insects, and the like, dying in this sacred field (kṣetra), quickly attain liberation, and not otherwise. Whether they be you or a Brāhmaṇa, those who obtain the six-syllabled mantra (ṣaḍakṣara) from you shall have their mantras perfected while living, and being disciplined, they shall even attain me. O Śaṅkara, whoever worships with devotion in this field by means of this mantra, I [shall be present]..."

"O Lord of Gods, even for one who is about to die and who touches a stone image or the like there, or into whose right ear you yourself shall personally impart this mantra, he shall become liberated and auspicious.

Having been told this, Śaṅkara spoke again: "O Lord of Gods, let the fruit characterized by liberation accrue to everyone in this field, which is difficult to attain in the three worlds, provided they are free from pride.

And we shall grant the supreme, excellent mantra to all those who are on the verge of death. After Viṣṇu had thus granted him that other boon which was desired by him previously, he vanished right there.

Since that place became the field of liberation (*mukti-kṣetra*) which purifies the three worlds, those who reside there with devotion, self-restrained for as long as they live, shall indeed become partakers of liberation; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. (33) [Thus ends the seventh chapter of the Śrī Agastisaṃhitā. Sutīkṣṇa said: How was the excellent ground of the mantra first established? And by whom was it installed? The lineage of gurus thus bestowed [the knowledge] upon the sage Vedavyāsa; through the mouth of Vedavyāsa, this mantra was revealed here upon the earth. The highly effulgent Vedavyāsa sat down with his disciples.

First, the sage spoke of the qualities of the guru and disciple to Śaunaka. "I shall explain what has been taught, if you wish to hear it here. Sutīkṣṇa said: "One who worships the deity, is peaceful, and is free from desire even for sense objects; one who knows the supreme self (*adhyātma*), is a proponent of Brahman (*brahmavādī*), and is skilled in the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras; a supreme Brāhmaṇa capable of both uplifting and destroying; one who knows mantras, knows the yantras of mantras, and knows their secrets; the number of preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), the materials for the fire-oblation (*homa*), and the places of austerity and their accomplishments as they were spoken by Brahmā in the past—all that which was spoken, I shall explain if you wish to hear it here."

Sutīkṣṇa said: "One who worships the deity, is tranquil, and is free from desire even for sense objects; one who knows the supreme self (*adhyātma*), is a proponent of Brahman (*brahmavādī*), and is skilled in the meaning of the Vedas and scriptures;

an excellent Brāhmaṇa capable of both uplifting and destroying; one who knows mantras, knows the yantras of mantras, and knows their secrets; one who has performed the preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), is accomplished in mantra, and knows its application;

an ascetic, truthful speaker, and householder—he is called a Guru. One who is a believer, devoted to the Guru, desirous of knowledge, and endowed with faith—[he is the one] from whom [the remedy for] the suffering arising from desire, anger, and so forth [should be sought]."
A Brahmin who desires to cross entirely over the ocean of worldly existence, being acquainted with the suffering of *bhava*, and who is devoid of longing for dharma, liberation, desire, or wealth;

or a twice-born man who is free from desire for the goals of dharma, wealth, and liberation; who constantly serves his guru through the virtues of mind, speech, and body; who is steadfast in the duties prescribed for his own stage of life (*āśrama*), ever pure, most observant of pure vows, virtuous, and a servant of the twice-born; as well as women devoted to their husbands, others born of inverse or natural order (*pratiloma-anuloma*), and the people of the world—[all these are described].

All those down to the Ḍāla class are eligible here, provided they are devoted to the duties of their own caste and are devotees of the Lord of All. The instruction for all of them is according to their respective castes:

[those who are] lazy, impure, afflicted, hypocritical, and likewise miserly; the poor, the diseased, the exalted, the healthy, and those greedy for enjoyments; those seized by envy and malice, the deceitful, and those who speak harshly; those who have acquired wealth through unjust means, those intent on the wives of others, those who are enemies of the learned, those who are ignorant yet consider themselves scholars, and those who have fallen from their vows.

Those who subsist on the remnants of others' meals, backbiters, the wicked, gluttons, those of cruel conduct, and those of cruel nature—these and other such most sinful, lowest of men, O best of sages, do not find release from the torments of hell. Those who, being greedy and deceitful, give [gifts] to these censured people, all that perishes like seeds sown in the sands. By those disciples who, out of childishness or pride, have insulted their gurus, there shall be a fall from the prosperity of sons, friends, wives, and the like, and they shall suffer for the harms they have done.

Those who are unable to endure the instruction of their guru must be restrained; such persons, even if they have been designated as disciples (*śiṣya*), are to be abandoned. If even those people who revile the deities were to be accepted [as disciples], they would become poor in this world, deprived of sons and wives. Those who are born in hells and among animals are the very bodies of these [transgressors]. Those most sinful and lowest of men who show contempt for their guru, and those who, out of delusion, insult their guru and speak harshly to him—for them, the state of being a pig occurs for a hundred births. Those who [show disrespect] to the guru...

Those who are treacherous, deluded, and constant evildoers—their merit, like their conduct, will undoubtedly be reduced to ashes. For the sake of liberation through Tārā and others, for liberation through the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī and others, and for the perfection of speech (*vāksiddhi*), one should place the speech-seed syllable at the end of the *praṇava*. Furthermore, for the sake of subjugating all through the Manmatha [seed-syllable], one should employ this triad again; placing Tārā at the end and Rāma at the beginning, one applies it for every purpose. This five-syllabled mantra is remembered as "Rāmāya Namaḥ. There is also the single-syllabled mantra "Rām," and another mantra, "Rām. [The mantra] "Caṃdrāṃ... [is also mentioned].

And from that very Bhadrānta, the Veda is again divided into fifty Mātṛkā-letters, each preceded by Rāma. Lakṣmī, Matha, and so forth, as well as the Praṇava (Oṃ), are present everywhere. Rāma, ending with Candra-Bhadrānta, is joined with the Heart-mantra in the dative case. This six-syllabled mantra is divided in many ways: it is established as one-fold, two-fold, three-fold, four-fold, five-fold, six-fold, seven-fold, eight-fold, and indeed in many other ways. This is the mantra which the teacher should impart according to the suitability of the Brāhmaṇas and others, having worshipped it according to the prescribed rite.
"Having established a new water-pot there, O Sage, whatever is given by the donor—whether made of clay or gold—in accordance with its capacity, so too should the mantra be bestowed.

(35) [Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Agastisaṃhitā. Sutīkṣṇa said: "O Brahmin, tell me what that yantra is, who created it himself, by which mantras it is empowered, how and where it should be drawn, and what is achieved by it? Agastya said: "O ascetic, from this yantra, which fulfills all desires, issues forth [the power to overcome] lust, anger, and other such afflictions."

Because it restrains [the mind] with long-lasting mechanical devices arising from it, they call it a *yantra*. O Rāma, one finds delight in worshipping within this. They say the *yantra* consists of mantra, for the deity has the form of mantra. If Rāma is worshipped through the *yantra*, he does not fail to be pleased immediately. When Śrī Rāma is worshipped in the *yantra* along with Sītā, he performs exactly whatever is desired, even without that supreme mantra. Just as the body is dear to the *jīva*, the mantra is said to be dear to Rāma. By propitiating the *yantra* and the mantra, one shall obtain whatever is desired. Having propitiated the mantra in the *yantra*...

O Sage, I shall describe the nature of the yantra as it was told by Brahmā in the past, which is used for the worship of all mantras and which propitiates Rāghava. First, having drawn a hexagon, one should then draw a circle; thereafter, one should draw eight petals, and then there should be a square. Endowed with all characteristics, clearly manifest, and pleasing to the mind, within that [square] one should very clearly write the seed-syllable (*bīja*) containing the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the ritual action (*karman*), which embraces the god of love (*manmatha*). Then, one should write those five seed-syllables.

O Sage, one should rotate [the mantra] again; with the ten-syllable mantra itself, one should encircle that very same [lotus]. One should write the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in sequence starting from the southeast corner.

Likewise, O Sage, one should write *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ* within the skull-marks at the corners. One should write the seed-syllable *hūṃ* at the tip of each corner and the vowels upon the filaments. Of this garland-mantra, there are forty-seven syllables; these should be placed six by six on the seven petals, and five on the pericarp. O ascetic, one should first encircle all of that with the consonants beginning with *ka*. The seed-syllable.

One should draw two [figures], Narasiṃha and Varāha, in the cardinal and intermediate directions starting from the east within a square earthen house; by properly worshipping this yantra, one attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Alternatively, one should write the *tāra* (the syllable Om) in the center, and in the six corners, the syllables of the root mantra in sequence. At the joints, one should place the *āṅga* (limb-mantras) and the *mānmatha* (the Kāma-bīja). The *māyā* (the syllable Hrīm) should be written on the lobes, and the vowels should be written upon the filaments. In these yantras, the *mālā-mantra* should indeed be inscribed in order as before, surrounded by the ten-syllabled mantra and the consonants beginning with *ka*.
One should draw the seed-syllables of Narasiṃha and Varāha in the cardinal and intermediate directions. Having drawn this other yantra on gold, silver, or birch-bark, one should begin the worship.

One should prescribe the ten-syllable mantra of Varāha as *hūṃ jānakīvallabhāya svāhā kṣauṃ hūṃ*. The mantra of Nṛsiṃha is remembered as follows: one should utter *hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ oṃ*, then the word *namo bhagavate*, then the words *raghunandanāya*, *rakṣoghna-viśadāya*, *madhurāya*, *prasannāya*, and *vadanāya*. These are the five adjectives.
One should say "namas" to Amitejas, then to Bala, Rāma, and Viṣṇu; this great mantra is declared to be the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) for men.

*Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ sītāyai svāhā*—this is the Sītā-mantra extracted from the heart. Having worshipped with devotion in this yantra along with its limbs (*aṅga*) and enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), and having made it into a pill, one should wear the yantra daily. It pacifies poverty and suffering, increases sons and grandsons, bestows sovereignty, effects subjugation, causes the destruction of enemies, grants knowledge, and produces happiness.
It wards off disease and sorrow; it is called the Vajrapañjara for the purpose of counteracting malevolent spells. O Sage, what need is there for much speaking? It bestows all accomplishments. (27)

[Thus ends the ninth chapter in the illustrious Agasti-saṃhitā. (9) Agastya said: O best of sages, listen as I describe the procedure for worship as it was told by Nārada to Vālmīki, the lord of munis—beginning with the worship of the door-guards—which bestows the fruit of all desired objects. I bow to Gaṇapati, to the Lord Śiva who has the sun as his crest-jewel, and to Kṣetrapāla, the Sustainer; for those deities who exist as the limbs and retinue of the door-guards of Śrī Rāma are the very roots from which all supernatural powers (*siddhis*) arise.

Having worshipped with devotion these deities of the doorway of Śrī Rāma— the Creator (Brahmā), the Lord of the House (Vāstospati), the House itself, Gaṅgā, Yamunā, the family deity, Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, as well as the two treasures Śaṅkha and Padma, Vāstospati, the Door, Lakṣmī, the Guru, and the Goddess of Speech— I bow down to Mahāmaṇḍūka and Kālāgnirudra, to Ādhāraśakti and Kūrma, to the Lord of Serpents, to the Earth, and again and again salutations to the Ocean of Milk and to Śvetadvīpa, Ratnādri, and Kalpa-vṛkṣa.

Salutations to the one who acts as a tree; salutations to the golden pavilion, to the Puṣpaka, and to the eight precious celestial chariots (vimānas); and to the excellent lion-throne. Immediately thereafter, [I bow] to the lotus resplendent like the rising sun. Then, in order, I salute Dharma and Jñāna; to Vairāgya from the southeast; to Aiśvarya; then to Adharma and Ajñāna in order from the east; likewise to Avairāgya and Anaiśvarya—salutations again and again. And to that which is above the solar orb at all times, [salutations] to the lunar orb, Oṃ!

Having meditated and contemplated thus, I bow down with great effort, worshipping with the mantra "Obeisance to the Fire-maṇḍala. Likewise, one should worship with "Obeisance, obeisance to Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas";

and to the Self, the Inner Self, the Supreme Self, and the Knowledge-Self. With the Praṇava and so forth, one should sacrifice in the center; thereby one becomes purified. After that, one should say "To Viṣṇu" and immediately after "To the Self of all beings. Then, "Salutation to Vāsudeva," followed by "Salutation to the Self who is the union of all and the lotus-throne. "Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the Self who is established as the Jāmadagnya (Paraśurāma). "Salutation to the final Rāma, and salutation again to him with Sītā. By means of this fixed yoga for establishing his presence, "Salutation to Rāma who is established as the six-faced one (Kārttikeya)," ending with "Salutation to the Fire. Then "Svāhā" at the end of the six-syllabled mantra beginning with the Śrī-bīja for Sītā. This is that mantra.

Salutation to Rāmāya-jyotis (the Light that is Rāma), who consists of the vowels ending with *sāmu-svāra*. Salutation to Vahni (Fire) ending with the vowels; salutation indeed to Kṛśānu (Fire) ending with the vowels and the syllable *īśvara*. Salutation to Śiras (the Head) ending with the syllable *oṃ* and to Śikhā (the Crest) consisting of the six vowels (*ṣaḍātman*). Thus, salutation to Ṣaḍaṅgātmarāmāya-jyotis. From Agni (Fire) onwards, in sequence, I bow to Ātman, Antarātman, Paramātman, and Jñānātman. Having proceeded through Nivṛtti, I bow to Pratiṣṭhā and Vidyā. I bow to Śānti and to those whose form consists of the powers (Śaktis) beginning with Ātman. Salutation to Vāsudeva.

Salutations again and again to the eternal Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Śrī, and Śānti; salutations to Prīti and Rati, and to the one whose second enclosure consists of Rāma. In front are Hanumān, Sugrīva, Bharata, Vibhīṣaṇa, Lakṣmaṇa, Aṅgada, Śatrughna, Jāmbavān, Dhṛṣṭi, Jayanti, Vijaya, Surāṣṭra, Rāṣṭravardhana, Akopa, Dharmapāla, and Sumantra as the eighth minister—to you all, who possess the form of Rāma, I bow down. [Salutations] to Indra and Yama...

Salutations again and again to the gods equipped with weapons; salutations to Vāyu, the giver of breath; and to that Rudra who is the primordial glory, salutations. Salutations to Brahmā, whose form is the interior, the guardian of the quarters, and the Self;

salutations to his weapons: to the thunderbolt (*vajra*), the spear (*śakti*), and the staff (*daṇḍa*). Salutations to the sword (*khaḍga*), the noose (*pāśa*), the banner (*dhvaja*), and the mace (*gadā*); salutations to the trident (*triśūla*), the lotus (*ambuja*), and the discus (*cakra*)—salutations to them all.
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Jābāli, Gautama, Bharadvāja, Kauśika, Vālmīki, and likewise Nārada—to these [sages] in the form of Rāma...

I bow down to you all: Nala, Nīla, Gavaya, Gavākṣa, Gandhamādana, Svarabhi, Mēṇḍa, and Vāli; one should worship them in this order. Obeisance to You, whose essence is the conch, discus, mace, lotus, bow, and arrows, and who are mounted upon Garuḍa; obeisance to Viśvaksena and the others. Constant obeisance to the Light, the embodiment of all sovereignty. Whatever action has been performed by mind, speech, or body, whether auspicious or inauspicious, may it all be for Your pleasure; obeisance to Rāma, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow. This secret [should be kept] constantly.

He who, concentrated at dawn, recites this *Rāmamāhātmya*, shall become a treasury of knowledge and sovereignty. He shall destroy ill fortune, cut through the flood of poverty, pacify all calamities, and bring the entire world under his control. Whoever, rising early each morning, recites this daily with the intention of offering it to Brahman, attains the eternal Brahman from which return is difficult to achieve. O best of sages Sutīkṣṇa, this *Nāradīya-stotra* should be recited with effort by those devoted to the worship of Rāma, as well as by Gaṇapati and all others who are the limbs of the door.

O Sage, these deities beginning with Gaṇapati—whether they possess the form of a Vedic metre or consist of the *praṇava* ending in *namaḥ*—should be worshipped with effort according to one's own capacity, using their respective names in the dative case, accompanied by sixteen, eleven, or five ritual offerings (*upacāras*). When these are worshipped, they in turn worship the worshipper. [Thus ends the tenth chapter of the Śrī Agasti Saṃhitā.
Agastya said: First, for the sake of attaining eligibility, one should daily purify the body; even external bathing in sacred waters (*tīrtha*) serves as a purification of the internal elements.

One should perform the *mātṛkā-nyāsa-yoga* according to the prescribed rules and purify it; thereafter, one should purify the materials for worship by means of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites. One should purify the vessels of worship and the conch shell by washing and so forth.

Being pure oneself, one should worship Puruṣottama with pure substances. When the Lord is propitiated in this manner, He becomes truly propitiated. Otherwise, everything is as useless as rain falling upon the sands of the ocean. If one is devoid of ritual purity (*śauca*) and the sipping of water (*ācamana*), then acts such as bathing and the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) will be fruitless; likewise, they would be so even in the absence of these [specific] requirements.

Having purified the materials for worship, both externally and internally, one should worship the conch; everything that is worthy of worship attains the state of being fit for worship. Then the worship of the worshipper shall be purifying, as will that which is performed for the sake of purification.

One should avoid impure acts of worship and means that are not purifying. Therefore, having bathed and performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), O Sage, one should perform the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* according to the Vaiṣṇava rite. Having performed the *tattva-nyāsa*, the *mūrti-pañjara*, the *ṛṣi-nyāsa*, the *chandas-nyāsa*, and likewise the *mantra-daivata-nyāsa*, one should perform the *nyāsa*.

Thus, one should perform the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) with their respective seed-syllables (bījākṣara), followed by meditation on the deity and then worship. After offering all that [as an oblation], one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind. Then, having informed the Lord of Devas, one should worship the retinue. Thus worshipped, the God grants all desires. Thereafter, one should indeed perform the external worship for the sake of worldly prosperity. Having properly drawn the altar (vedikā), one should have a mandala prepared there using flour of rice and blue, yellow, white, and black powders. One should draw [the design].

An eight-petaled lotus, surrounded by a square, with a six-cornered [figure] in the center of the pericarp and a circle at the tip of each corner—this is the most excellent [mandala]. Then, having worshipped the mandala, which is adorned with beautiful lines and the object of accomplishment (sādhya), one should place a lion-throne there. It should be made variegated here and there with moon-canopies, banners, and archways on all sides, as well as on the walls, pillars, and within the house.
In such a beautifully adorned place, filled with every auspiciousness, surrounded by virtuous women, householders, and attendants, while they sing, dance, and speak.

If Raghunātha himself is properly propitiated there with various musical instruments such as the *bherī*, *mṛdaṅga*, flute, and cymbals (*kāṃsyatāla*), accompanied by hymns of praise, the Blessed One will become pleased. Having prepared a canopy of flowers (*puṣpajālikā*) using various kinds of blossoms, and having also used *tulasī*, lotuses, water for the feet (*pādya*), and many types of garlands;

and having placed before him his own vessel filled with pure water at the southern holy site (*tīrtha*), he should set aside that turbid water and employ it for the ritual enjoyments (*bhoga*). All other articles of worship should likewise be placed right in front.

One should cast [the offerings] beneath the altar for the propitiation of the God upon a comfortable seat fashioned from a spread of *kuśa* grass, tiger skin, or cloth. Having sat down, purified and assuming the state of a devotee (*bhogī*), one should perform the worship.

Likewise, having placed upon one's head a garland of *āmalaka* fruits, a proper lotus wreath, and a garland of *tulasī* from the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*), one should mark one’s limbs with the sandalwood paste from that same *nirmālya*, using the names of the Lord.

O best of the twice-born, one should likewise place His weapons on one’s arms with that very same substance; whether one is most sinful or sinless, or even all-knowing or ignorant, [one should do so].

Thus, one would undoubtedly become qualified for this rite of worship. Having drawn a lotus, a svastika, a bhadraka, or other such forms, and having bowed to Vināyaka at the two feet, one should place Sarasvatī on the left side and Durgā on the right side as before, and again Kṣetrapa. Then, reciting "Oṃ astrāya phaṭ," one should brandish the right hand. Thereafter, one should meditate upon that very deity within the three locations—effulgent, imperishable, consisting of truth, knowledge, and bliss—and for the protection of the self, [one should visualize] a rampart of fire all around oneself against bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas.

Immediately after performing those two [rites], the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should smear [the area] all around with water, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), consecrated with the fire-seed syllable (vahnibīja) and the weapon-mantra (astra), for the sake of removing fear and obstacles. The wise should contemplate the individual soul (jīva), which is the size of the tip of a needle, as being born from the root-stalk of Brahmā (brahmakaṇḍa) and having the heart-lotus (hṛdambuja) as its stalk. It should be led by the Haṃsa-mantra to the Supreme (Para) situated at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths]. Having united it there according to the rule, one should then perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). As for the elements—earth, water, fire, air, and ether—one should [dissolve them] back into that from which they were produced.

Furthermore, for the sake of attaining the Puruṣa, one should contemplate the Jīva and then the Ātman. For the perfection of the body of the Jīva, there is the purification of the elements that constitute the form of the body by means of the seeds of Wind (vāyu), Fire (agni), and Nectar (sudhā). Having restrained the vital breaths (prāṇas) through the fifty Mātṛkās, one should dry up the body of the Self and then burn it.

Having again flooded that body, one should bring the Jīva back here. With the Jīva, one should again contemplate the Ātman for the attainment of the Puruṣa, for the perfection of the body of the Jīva, and for the establishment of its very nature as the Self.

For the purpose of bringing [the deity] forth and leading [him] back, one should utter "I am He" (So'ham). This is called *Bhūtaśuddhi* (Purification of the Elements), which effects the purpose of the Name. For one who performs recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), and other rites without *Bhūtaśuddhi*, all such actions, however firmly established they may be, become fruitless. They know that approaching the temple, following after Lord Hari with devotion, circumambulating him, and the cleansing of his feet constitute purification for the hands. Likewise, the lifting of flowers for the purpose of worship for Lord Hari—done solely out of devotion—is declared to be the purification of all [other] purifications. That by which the Name is...

The recollection of Śrī Rāmacandra’s virtues and the chanting of his names with devotion are considered the purification of speech; likewise, listening to his stories and witnessing his festivals are declared here to be the proper purification of the ears and eyes respectively. Wearing the water from his feet, his *nirmālya*, and even his garlands is said to be the purification of the head for one who bows to Hari. O ascetic, smelling the fragrance of the flowers and other offerings used in worship is prescribed as the purification of the sense of smell for Ananta. [This applies to] leaves, flowers, and so forth.

Whatever has been offered at the pair of Rāma’s feet becomes pure by its very nature; whether it be held by oneself now or previously, whatever was offered to Viṣṇu, that alone is the purifier in this world, for it shall cleanse everything. (47) [Thus ends the eleventh chapter of the Śrī Agastisaṃhitā.

(11) Agastya said: Now, therefore, the sequence of the Mātṛkā-nyāsa is recited here; having restrained the vital breaths, one should assign the Ṛṣi, Chandas, Deity, Bīja, and Śakti to the head, mouth, and so forth.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the heart, the secret parts, and the feet; one should place each vowel individually upon the lines of the fingers of the hands. One should place the *praṇava* (oṃ) on both palms and also on the backs of the hands.

The five groups of five consonants beginning with *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, and *śa*, ending with the short and long vowels, are to be placed. The ten letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *la* are to be placed at the beginning and end of the thumbs and so forth, as well as on the palms and the backs of the hands.

Thus, the arrangement for the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) occurs. [The mantras are placed] in the heart, the head, the crest-lock (*śikhā*), all the limbs, and the eyes, as well as in the directions and the weapon (*astra*).

*Namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *hūṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and likewise *astrāya phaṭ*—these are the "sprouts" (*pallava*) of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). In that context, the placement (*nyāsa*) of each respective limb is joined with its corresponding sprout, ending in the dative case, and applied to those specific locations. Now follows the internal *mātṛkā-nyāsa*: the arrangement of the fifty letters occurs in sequence upon the petals situated in the lotuses of the throat, heart, navel, secret place, anus, and between the eyebrows—consisting of sixteen, twelve, ten, six, four, and two petals respectively. One letter is placed upon each [petal].

O Sage, one should place [the letters] at the end of the petals; having thus placed them within, one should then place them externally with the mind: on the head, face, forehead, eyes, ears, nostrils, the pair of cheeks, as well as on the upper and lower lips, and on the upper and lower rows of teeth. One should place the sixteen vowels on the head and the mouth. The two *ka*-groups (ka, kha) should be placed on the two arms and the five joints of the hands. Likewise, one should place the two *ṭa*-groups (ṭa, ṭha) on the joints and tips of the feet. The *pa*-group (pa, pha) should be placed on the pair of sides, the back, the navel, and the abdomen. [The remaining letters] from the root of the heart, the hips, the flanks, and from the heart onwards to the hands and feet...

One should apply the pervasive [mantra] to the belly and the face; the placement of the fifty syllables is prescribed in due order. [The mantra] beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, preceded by *saviṃdu* (with the bindu) or devoid of the bindu, is said to be placed first with the seed-syllables of Māyā, Lakṣmī, and Kāma. One should place [the names]: to Keśava and Kīrti, and likewise to Nārāyaṇa and Kānti; to Mādhava and Tuṣṭi—one should say "namas"; then to Govinda and Puṣṭi; then Viṣṇu and Dhṛti; then to Madhusūdana and Śānti; to Trivikrama and Kriyā; and to Vāmana...

One should say "Salutation to Dayā (Compassion) and Śrīdhara," and likewise "Salutation to Medhā (Intelligence) and Hṛṣīkeśa. One should say "Salutation to Harṣa (Joy)," and likewise "Salutation to Padmanābha and Śraddhā (Faith). Having said "Salutation to Vāsudeva and Lajjā (Modesty)," one should then say "Salutation to Saṃkarṣaṇa and Lakṣmī. One should utter "Salutation to Pradyumna and Sarasvatī," and "Salutation to Rati and Prīti. Then, at the end of the syllable *kha*, one should say "Salutation to Aniruddha and Rati. Furthermore, one should assign [the mantras] to Cakrin (the Wielder of the Discus) and Vijayā, to Śārṅgin (the Wielder of the Bow) and Gadin (the Wielder of the Mace), and then to Durgā and Prabhā, and finally to Khaḍgin (the Wielder of the Sword).

One should say "Salutation" to Tyāga, Śaṅkhin, Caṇḍa, and likewise to Halin; to Vāṇī and Muśalin. Then, after that, to Vilāsinī, Śūlin, and Vijayā. One should say [salutation] to Pāśin, Viraja, and likewise to Aṅkuśin; to Viśva, Mukunda, and Vinada. Likewise, salutation to Nandaja, Sunanda, and Nandina. Salutation to Nara, Ṛddhi, and similarly to Naraka-ghna; to Samṛddhi, Hari, Śuddhi, Kṛṣṇa, and Bhukta. Salutation to Sattva, Buddhi, Sātvata, and Mati.

One should utter: "Obeisance to Śauri, Cakṣu, Kṣamā, Śūra, and Carama; to Janārdana, Uma, and then to Śārṅgadhara; to Kledinī, Viśvamūrti, and Klinna; likewise obeisance to Vaikuṇṭha, and similarly obeisance to Vasudā; to Puruṣottama, Vasudhā, Para, and Vālin; to Bālānuja, Parāyaṇa—thus one should utter; to Vala, Sūkṣma, Sandhyā, and Vṛṣaghna; to Vṛṣa, Prajñā, Haṃsa, and Prabhā; to Vārāha and Niśā."

Then, one should assign [the mantras] to *Cavimalāya*, *Avadattāya*, *Amoghāya*, *Narasiṃhāya*, and *Vidyute* respectively. The sequence is: the seed-syllable of Kāma (*Klīm*), the letters of the Mātṛkā alphabet, "One Deity," "One Śakti," and "Salutation" (*Namaḥ*). Furthermore, one should place Keśava and Kīrti at the end with "Salutation. This is the prescribed rule for the locations such as the head, face, and chest. The sequence is: the syllable *Oṃ*, the seed-syllable of Ravi (*Rām*), the letters of the Mātṛkā alphabet, "One Deity," "One Śakti," and "Salutation. This is the Nyāsa beginning with Keśava; by the mere performance of this Nyāsa, embodied beings [attain their goal].

It bestows the state of immortality; this is the truth, the truth—of this there is no doubt. I shall now describe the *sutīkṣṇa-tattva* (the extremely sharp reality); listen further to it. By the mere performance of this *tattva-nyāsa*, one truly becomes that very reality itself. The letters from *ka* onwards are to be arranged in reverse order (*pratiloma*) and designated as "all" (*sarva*). They are established at the end of the *praṇava* (Oṃ) preceded by *namaḥ parāya*. Having placed the *jīva*, *prāṇa*, *buddhi*, and likewise *ahaṃkāra* along with *namaḥ*, one should assign them to the entire body and the heart. One should also assign the sense organs, beginning with hearing, to the head, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the heart, the generative organ, and the feet.

One should again place the five organs of knowledge—ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose—along with form and the other [objects], each in its respective location within the embodied being. Likewise, one should duly place the primary organs of action—speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals—in their respective locations. Furthermore, those who are proficient in ritual placement (nyāsa) have declared that one should place ether, air, fire, water, and earth in the head, face, heart, genitals, and feet, respectively, just as before. This is indeed the method taught by Śāṇḍilya, Rāma, Vasiṣṭha, and Caraja.

One should [place] the ten-syllable mantra *kṣauṃ* preceded by the Praṇava as before. Having placed the triad of circles—consisting of the heart-lotus, moon, sun, and fire, each endowed with its own digits (*kalā*)—within the heart itself, one should likewise place Vāsudeva and the others:

Parameṣṭhin, Puruṣa, Viśva, Nivṛtti, Nārāyaṇa, and Nṛsiṃha, preceded by Sarvaka and Upāsya. Then, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) on the head, face, heart, secret parts, and feet. Thereafter, one should place that [mantra] with the self-mantra (*ātmanamantra*) according to its respective position. Therefore, because it is the cause for attaining even that which is otherwise unattainable, [one should worship it].

Those who know the truth have said that *nyāsa* (ritual placement) is [the means by which] you are placed elsewhere; whoever performs the *nyāsa* of the principles (*tattva*) certainly attains service (*sevā*). For the Blessed One enters and dwells within the self, because He is the essence and everything is established in Him. That *nyāsa* of the cage of His forms is for the sake of accomplishing those forms; listen with a single-minded heart to that wherein there is no other fruit. One should say "Salutation to the Blessed Vāsudeva," taking the single syllable from the mantra of the Lord, "Oṃ Ādidevasya," and then each individual syllable.

In the same manner, for the mantra known as Śrī Rāma, one should take two syllables at a time from each of the ten names of Viṣṹṇu, and likewise from the names of the Sun. Then there should be *oṃ*, then a vowel, then a syllable of Vāsudeva, then a syllable of the Śrī Rāma mantra, and then the names beginning with Keśava and Dhātṛ, ending with *namaḥ*. These names of the Sun are to be deposited through the method of *nyāsa* on the forehead, navel, heart, throat, sides, armpits, shoulders, back, and hump, in due order, followed by Keśava and the rest.

One should utter the names: Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana, Trivikrama, Vāmana, Śrīdhara is remembered as the ninth, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and the Lord Dāmodara. O best of sages, these are the twelve names of Viṣṇu. Dhātṛ, Aryamā, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, Bhaga, Vivasvat, Indra, Pūṣan, Parjanya is remembered as the tenth, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viṣṇu—these are the twelve names of the Self. This is the Nyāsa of the cage of His forms.

Beneficial [is this practice] ordained by Parameṣṭhin: one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the syllables of the root mantra upon the head, between the eyebrows, the heart, the secret place, the feet, and the breasts, as well as the six-limbed nyāsa. Having performed the placement in this manner according to the rules, one becomes Nārāyaṇa manifest; fevers, diseases, malevolent spells, and the like go to their destruction, and not otherwise. So too do ghosts, spirits, piśācas, brahmarākṣasas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and ḍākinīs—not even able to look upon a single syllable. The wise man who performs this placement becomes Rāma himself, manifest. There is nothing more purifying or meritorious than this.

[Salutation to the Guru. (65) [Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the glorious Agasti-saṃhitā. (12) Agastya said: Having prepared vessels of excellent quality for the sake of worship with due care, and having purified the conch with the Astra-mantra and placed it upon its base, one should worship Fire, the Sun, and the Moon with their respective seed-syllables (*bījas*) accompanied by the fruits of the *tattvas*.

One should worship those respective deities within the bases, the conch, and the sacred waters (*tīrtha*) according to the number of their *kalās*—ten, twelve, and sixteen—invoking the sacred waters with the *Tīrthāvāhana-mantras* and performing the worship.

Furthermore, with devotion, one should offer perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, incense, lamps, and so forth, and display the conch mudrā as well as the mudrā known as Gāruḍa. Having diligently rendered it supreme, one should contemplate that purifying [water]. One should sprinkle it upon the head of the Deity, as well as upon the ritual materials and oneself. One should thus effect the purification of all things through inspection (*avekṣaṇa*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), gazing (*vīkṣaṇa*), striking (*tāḍana*), and worship (*arcana*). Only when purified does every means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) become fit for worship. This applies likewise to the water in the *argha* vessel for the purpose of offering, for the *madhuparka*, and for the purpose of sipping (*ācamana*).

One should place four vessels before oneself; first, one should prepare the conch. Then, having consecrated auspicious water in the *argha* vessel and the *pādya* vessel, one should place therein for the sake of accomplishing the purpose: fragrance, flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), barley, the tips of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds in the *argha* vessel. In the *pādya* vessel, one should place millet (*śyāmāka*) and *dūrvā* grass; for the successful preparation of the *pādya*, one should employ lotus and *viṣṇukrāntā*. Likewise, O Sage, one should offer nutmeg (*jātīphala*), cloves (*lavaṅga*), and *kakkola* as the *ācamana* (water for sipping). These are highly recommended for the *ācamana*.

A honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) shall be prepared with curd, honey, and ghee. One should perform the ritual bath (*snāna*) with the *Puruṣasūkta* and with pure water from a conch shell. Furthermore, one should bathe [the deity] separately with milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, and sugar-candy;
likewise with coconut water, the juice of the palmyra fruit, various fragrant substances, scented water, and sugarcane juice.

Having perfumed it with excellent camphor and other aromatics, one should sprinkle [the image] a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand times—or as many times as one’s capacity—with that water. O best of the Raghus, one should fill the conch shell with that very same water and with beautiful flowers.

Then, with single-minded devotion, one should bathe him with pure water while intermittently perfuming him with incense of black aguru. For the sake of sovereignty and the attainment of a kingdom, one should perform this consecration daily for a year with care;
by doing so, one becomes a king, and not otherwise. Having offered water for sipping (ācamanīya), one should clothe him in two garments, followed by the gift of ornaments along with an upper cloth.
Then, having given a sacred thread (yajñopavīta), one should respectfully offer sandalwood paste, flowers, perfumes, and various garlands, as well as incense.

The lamp, the food offering (naivedya), betel, circumambulation, and prostration—these are the sixteen services (upacāras) in worship. These consist of the eleven beginning with invocation (āvāhana) and the five others;

one should perform the worship day and night with these services, as well as with musical instruments, perfumes, and other offerings prepared according to one's capacity and devotion. Having thus worshipped the door, the pedestal, the deities of the quarters, and so forth, and having propitiated Rāma before them according to the rules with all the services, the limbs, the deities of the enclosures (āvaraṇas), and the other weapons should be worshipped. In this manner, [one should worship] perfectly...

One should worship Rāma—who is worthy of being propitiated along with his limbs, retinue, and vehicle—with great effort and by bowing down properly; and one should also worship the yantra with its mantras diligently and correctly.

In this very manner, O descendant of Raghu, one should worship Rāghava in the fire during homa and other rites, and likewise propitiate him in water during tarpaṇa and other ceremonies. Furthermore, worship of Śrī Rāmacandra performed upon a Śālagrāma stone or with *tulasī* leaves is millions of millions of times more meritorious than that performed before an image, on the ground, in the fire, in the sun, or in water.

Having placed [the deity] even within his heart as a secret, one should worship with Tulasī leaves using the ritual services (upacāras). One should ring the bell and offer water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) to the God; in between each [offering], having offered each respective item again and again, one should present them. One should not worship with buds, fallen flowers, those that are withered, nor even with blood, nor with unworthy flowers, petals, or leaves.
With whatever flower, leaf, or petal, having brought it from wherever it may be and regardless of where it originated—for the sake of worldly existence and for the sake of life—[one should worship].

One may worship Hari constantly at a place deemed unfit; by doing so, one obtains that same fruit which is attained by the gift of a cow at the Gaṅgā for three hundred divine years. One should offer even a leaf, a flower, or a fruit as a means of worshipping Rāma. Listen to the meritorious fruit obtained by him who has thus worshipped Him: he attains all that merit—there is no doubt—which is gained by the gift of a thousand cows at Kurukṣetra, the Gaṅgā, Prayāga, or Puruṣottama, whether he offers it in its entirety or partially, provided it is offered with devotion.
Whether it be once or even daily, one should offer much worship to Hari; for what is the use of visiting sacred fords or other various gifts that have been described?
