If one is incapable of performing formal worship, one should give the means for worship; if one is unable to give those, one should at least perform the act of seeing [the deity]. O best of sages, this leads to the crossing of the ocean of worldly existence for the sake of the gods; if not even one of these exists, he shall certainly go to hell, and not otherwise. If one performs the worship of the deity in any way whatsoever outside of the prescribed rules, there is no fruit for him, just as a great deal of water poured upon ashes. He who worships according to the injunctions...

If one performs worship with materials brought by others out of devotion, one obtains only half the fruit of the rite; one does not obtain the full fruit. However, the wise person who, with devotion and effort, personally procures all the ritual materials and performs the worship, shall obtain the full fruit. One should bring flowers from trees planted by others and perform worship, while respectfully displaying the various corresponding mudrās. Having made the deity gracious, having caused it to become present, and having invoked its presence, one should worship it. At that time, one should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa (the infusion of limbs) for the deity’s vital breaths as well as its senses. If it is done in this manner...

One who worships Rāma attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (51) [Thus ends the thirteenth chapter of the Śrī Agasti Saṃhitā. (13) Agastya said: Having invoked the Deity into the fire consecrated according to the rules, one should worship Him by the very procedure previously described, including the limbs (*aṅga*), the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), and the vehicle (*vāhana*). I shall declare that procedure by which the desired fruit is accomplished; those by whom it is performed as ordained become partakers of the fruit. Of all desired things, this is the way; otherwise, it is not so. [Only those whose wealth is acquired through righteous means...]

With those means, one should perform acts such as giving, fire-offerings (homa), and worship; for even if a twice-born performs them with devotion, he does not fall [from his state] otherwise. Having leveled the ground site with intervals of six or four finger-breadths, one should likewise fashion a square pedestal of that same measure. Then, having made the four side-areas within each direction according to these characteristics, one should construct a girdle (mekhalā) on the outside. It should be twelve, eight, or four finger-breadths in measure according to one's own limbs; thus its height and length should be exactly four finger-breadths. Its length and height—

By adding four units to the form [of the pit] in sequence, one should fashion three sets of four; thus shall be the order of the girdles (*mekhalā*). One should fashion the *yoni* in the western part of the pit according to its characteristics: resembling an *aśvattha* leaf, slightly elevated within the pit, and it should be six, four, and two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) respectively from top to bottom. Furthermore, that *yoni* is ten finger-breadths in width. Its base, stalk, and tip are six, four, and three [finger-breadths] respectively; such is the measurement in finger-breadths, and this is the characteristic of the pit (*kuṇḍa*).

This method for a one-cubit pit has been demonstrated; a two-cubit pit should likewise be made by doubling [the measurements], including the girdles (*mekhalā*) and the navel, or else the pit may consist of only a single girdle. Such is the characteristic of a circular pit as well, for rites performed in brief. In the center of a square one-cubit pit, having fixed a mark, O Sage, one should rotate a cord all around it. Alternatively, having established [marks] at the corners, one should direct the excess toward the four directions. This, then, is the circular pit; from that [arises] the semi-circle.

In the northern direction, from the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should mark the middle point at half a part plus a quarter-part outward from the eastern and western sides. Having fixed that point, one should rotate [the cord] to form this "half-moon" shape, which bestows auspiciousness. O storehouse of penance, for a circular pit, there should be eight petals upon the girdles; this lotus-shaped pit grants all fruits. For a hundred oblations, it should be one cubit (aratni) in measure; for fifty, it should be the size of a fist. For a thousand, ten thousand, half a lakh, or even a full lakh, it increases respectively by five finger-breadths (aṅgulas) up to the measure of one cubit.

For a *kuṇḍa* used in ten million oblations (*koṭihoma*), it should be half of that; for six million, one-eighth. Measured in fist-widths (*muṣṭi*), they are ten, twelve, and sixteen respectively; in that same order, the first girdle (*mekhalā*) for those of noble lineage should be [one part]. For the second and third girdles, one should specify three parts and two parts respectively. For all *kuṇḍas*, the first girdle should be made by increasing two finger-breadths (*aṅguli*) [per unit]; the others should be as before, even in the case of three parts. The neck (*kaṇṭha*) and lip (*oṣṭha*) should be one barley-corn (*yava*) thick; in a *kuṇḍa* measuring one cubit (*kara*), the neck should be six barley-corns thick, and in a *kuṇḍa* measuring one span (*ratni*), [the neck should be]...

For a *māṇaka* [measuring] four *yavas*, one should specify the neck (*kaṇṭha*) as being only a *muṣṭi* [in circumference]. For all *kuṇḍas*, the first girdle (*mekhalā*) should be made by increasing [the measurement] by two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), while the others should be as before, increased by a third part.
The lip (*oṣṭha*) of the neck should be one *yava* in measure; for a neck measuring one *aratni*, it should likewise be specified as four *yavas*.

For all measurements of *kuṇḍas*, the neck must be carefully constructed by those desiring the fruits of enjoyment and liberation, increasing by two finger-breadths [for each size]. [The girdles are] *sāttvikī*, *rājasī*, and *tāmasī*.

In sequence, there should be the first, then the second, and then the third; one should fashion them from the beginning, the end, and the middle according to the dimensions of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). According to the prescribed measurement of finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), it should be made double or quadruple in size by the rules of the number of oblations (*homa*). One should provide a *sruva* ladle for the purpose of the oblation, characterized by all the proper marks and measuring the length of an arm. Having first fashioned a square [pit] of seven or five finger-breadths in sequence, the circular portion (*varta*) should be one-third of that; know that it is within that.

Having dug it to a measured depth, equal on all sides—horizontally, upwards, and downwards—one should clear the exterior. One should fashion its beautiful girdle (*mekhalā*) using one-fourth of an *aṅgula* for the lines and half of that at the end. It should be made with a width of one part, surrounded by one *aṅgula*. Its tip or opening should be one and a half *aṅgulas*, or four *aṅgulas* in width, or even five *aṅgulas*; its middle portion should be three *aṅgulas* and very beautiful. There should be a hollow in the region of the jar (*kuṃbha*) as far as the little finger can enter.

A sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be constructed according to one's preference, adorned with various designs, square in shape, measuring one cubit, and very beautiful. O Sage, one should fashion two beautiful *sruk* and *sruva* ladles made of wood from the *duṣṭaka*, *kaṃśa*, or *vṛtta* trees, each two fingers wide; or, for a concise fire-sacrifice (*homakarma*), they may be made of *palāśa* leaves or *śuttha* wood. Then, one should properly prepare the site of the pit in the northwest (the direction of Vāyu), where there is an eight-petaled lotus surrounded by three circles representing the Moon, Sun, and Fire.

The wise practitioner should act in this manner: having established a square outside, he should place a hexagon within the pericarp. Yellow should be applied in the east, white in the west, and likewise in the north; red in the south, black in the southeast (Agni), and pale-pink (pāṭala) situated in the fire-quarter; blue in the southwest (Nairṛta), smoke-colored (dhūmra) in the northwest (Vāyu), and white (gaura) in the northeast—this is the sequence for the eight petals. One should properly draw the conch, discus, mace, lotus, bow, and arrows upon the maṇḍala with pigments, and there, O Rāma, one should worship Him. Having worshipped in the same way within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should offer oblations, O Sage.

First, having sat upon a comfortable seat, one should perform the *agnimukha* (opening of the fire-rite). Having restrained the vital breaths (*prāṇāyāma*), one should mentally recite the mantra with undistracted mind as long as the breath circulates through all the limbs while remaining motionless. Having drawn lines on the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) or in the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), three vertical and three horizontal lines, one should invoke the fire-mantra. After sprinkling [the site] and bringing it forward, one should respectfully place the seat-grass (*viṣṭara*). There, one should contemplate the Fire born from the "village-dharma" (sexual union) of the Lord Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī during her fertile season. [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]

According to that very procedure, one should bring fire even from the house of an *āhitāgni* and establish it there; having carefully washed it with *kuśa* grass, one should have it inspected by those learned in sacrifice and wash it again with sacrificial wood. Then, having performed *prāṇāyāma*, one should strew *kuśa* blades around it according to the rules prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, O Sage, [worshipping] Vāsudeva and the others. The knower of the ritual (*tantravit*) should duly prepare the vessels with the two-fold mantra, look at them with a *pavitra*, and arrange them face upwards. Having sprinkled the vessel again and filled the *pavitra* with auspicious water, he should place the *akṣa*...

That strainer and the other three types [of vessels] should be placed in the northern direction; that vessel is called *praṇītā* by the wise. There, one should worship the Lord Viṣṇu and Brahmā, and one should worship the Sun.

Having consecrated the clarified butter (*ājya*) according to the rules, saying "it is well-prepared" (*svasaṃpannam*), one should perform for the fire the rites beginning with the *garbhadāna* and ending with the *vivāha*. One should offer eight oblations for each individual rite into the worshipped fire, ending with the word *vauṣaṭ*. Having completed that, one should begin another rite and conclude it at its end. Thus, when the fire is well-prepared...

One should offer the *caru* oblation while reciting the *Ṣaṇmukha-mantra*. Beginning with the placing of the fuel (*idhmādhāna*), one should perform the *agnimukha* and the two *ājyabhāga* offerings. Then, one should worship the descendant of Raghu (Rāma) in the fire using the invocation mantras.

One should offer sixteen oblations each of *samidh*, clarified butter (*ājya*), and *caru*, using the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). O Sage, one should likewise offer three oblations to the attendants (*parivāra*) beginning with Vināyaka. Furthermore, one should offer oblations to the deities who are the guardians of the gates and their attendants. Having offered the oblation of clarified butter there for the attainment of those respective goals, one should offer oblations with the specific materials for each, according to one's desire.

Having first offered oblations to Hara, the door-keepers, the pedestal-deities, and the guardians of the quarters, one should then offer separate oblations of clarified butter (ājya) to the limbs (aṅgas) and the Vaiṣṇava deities. Then, O best of sages, having performed the sviṣṭakṛt offering with ghee and having properly sprinkled water all around according to the rite, one should perform the purification with the praṇītā water and give the sacrificial fee (brahmadakṣiṇā) to the Brahmin priest according to one's own means, free from greed and delusion. Thereafter, having dismissed the Brahmin priest, one should feed the other Brahmins; finally, one should re-unite the Lord who was situated within the fire back into one's own self.

Having contemplated [the deity] as having become one with himself, he should recite the *svastivācana*; being consecrated by the benedictory words of the learned, he shall become happy. Then, having consumed the remnant of the oblation in a quantity equal to a hen’s egg, he should offer its *bali* with the *Gāyatrī* mantra while facing left. Even in the presence of the deity, whether for daily (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*) rites, this is remembered as the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*). Everywhere, for the sake of prosperity, one should perform the *abhyudaya-śrāddha* and the sowing of sprouts (*aṅkurāropaṇa*) at the very beginning of the rite.

[Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the glorious Agastya-saṃhitā. (14) Agastya said: O Sage, I shall now describe the ritual application (*prayoga*) that grants the desires of all four [classes of practitioners]; by practicing this even one of meager fortune obtains his desired fruit. Having properly prepared the portion for the fire according to the rules, like a liberated soul, one should then invoke Him and worship with five or sixteen distinct articles of worship. One should duly kindle the fire using fuel-sticks of *pālāśa*, *aśvattha*, *khadira*, *udumbara*, and *vaṭa*.

O Rāghava, one should worship there properly with the *gyāñjaka* and *vapavedhana* mantras, and likewise offer a hundred thousand oblations (*lakṣa-homa*). Or, having recited [the mantra] a hundred thousand times, or even half of that, or a tenth part of that, by offering oblations of sesame seeds or lotuses, one attains whatever is desired. By worshipping the fire and offering oblations of *vilva* flowers, sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) shall arise. By offering oblations of *pālāśa* flowers, one becomes wise and a knower of the gods.

O ascetic, by using *dūrvā*, *guḍūcī*, or unbroken grains (*akṣata*)—even for each individually—one certainly becomes free from disease and long-lived; and by using sandalwood water, one becomes exceedingly fierce (*pratyugra*).

Having offered oblations with *jājī* flowers sprinkled [with ghee], one shall bring even a king under one's control. Meditating upon Rāma as being composed of the self (*ātman-maya*), one should likewise remember Sītā as Rati. In all applications for subjugation (*vaśya*) and in rites such as recitation and fire-offerings (*japa-homa*), one should worship with devotion and remember Rāma as the one who causes men to ascend [to liberation]. By offering *lāja* oblations, the practitioner obtains a suitable maiden; by offering oblations of fresh red lotuses, he attains his desired wealth. By properly offering blue lotuses, he shall bring the entire world under his control. [One should worship] Rāma according to the prescribed rule... (Note: The final fragment "jva(-)" appears to be a corruption or truncation of the source text.)
One who knows the application of the *litognau* [mantra], by offering milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with honey and molasses, will undoubtedly attain universal sovereignty and erudition.

By offering sesame seeds, rice, and clarified butter (*ājya*), one attains kingship over the world for as long as a year. One should recite [the mantra] six thousand times every day and offer oblations into the fire ten times that amount, using ghee as the fuel. This very person becomes the leader of all in the world. Likewise, by offering *vilva* flowers, buds, and even *vilva* fruits, one obtains [success].

O Sage, a practitioner of mantras who worships Rāmacandra in his solar orb for one year, reciting the mantra with single-minded devotion from sunrise until sunset, shall attain a fruit difficult even for the gods to obtain. Through that merit, he shall become a sovereign free from suffering and the most excellent among his subjects. On the full moon night, he should observe this vow from sunrise to sunset for a year, performing recitation (japa), fire-offerings (homa), and other rites for the Lord; he should perform the recitation at night and the fire-offering during the day, or otherwise as prescribed.

Having fed the Brahmins on each day, one should complete this vow. That person who performs this vow, which consists of both Soma and Sūrya, obtains enjoyment and liberation in this world; of this there is no doubt. One who desires to bring the desired world under control should offer oblations into the fire with jewels, lotuses, bandhūka flowers, and likewise with jewel-lotuses.
One who seeks royal sovereignty and enjoyments should, with single-minded devotion, offer oblations on a mountain with lotuses or bilva blossoms for twelve months, O Sage, [near] the ocean.

A man who performs one hundred thousand recitations (*japa*) on a riverbank becomes invisible; by offering oblations of milk-rice mixed with clarified butter, he becomes a treasury of knowledge. One whose sovereignty has been exhausted should perform *japa* of the mantra one hundred thousand times while subsisting on vegetables and staying within the water, and offer oblations ten thousand times with *bilva* leaves; then his own sovereignty returns to him, without a doubt. Having fasted and stayed within the waters of the Ganges or similar rivers, one should propitiate Rāma and perform one hundred thousand recitations, offering oblations ten thousand times with lotuses, sesame seeds, or *bilva* flowers smeared with the three sweets (*madhuratrika*); [the result is] kingship.

Even one of meager fortune attains prosperity; even the status of a secondary servant becomes desired by others. Having propitiated Rāma according to the rules, when the fire has been duly worshipped, one should perform recitation (*japa*). Even if the solar disc is situated in water, one should offer oblations (*homa*) with stalks of sugarcane. O ascetic, during the autumn season, one obtains the royal fortune (*rājyalakṣmī*). In the month of Vaiśākha, beholding the sun as Rāghava without blinking, fasting and observing silence, one should perform a hundred thousand recitations in the midst of the five fires. Having offered oblations with lotuses amounting to a tenth part of that number, one will certainly become a sovereign emperor. Standing in water during the month of Māgha, [one should worship] Kṛṣṇa...

Eating only wild roots and fruits, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred thousand times and offer oblations of consecrated milk-rice (pāyasa) into the fire ten thousand times. For the sake of obtaining sons and grandsons, the woman should consume the remainder of this.
A son or grandson equal to Śrī Rāma will be born to her. If the counselor is oppressed or insulted by powerful enemies, he should then say "Kill! Kill! while uttering the names of those foes.

Meditating upon the pure Lord of the Raghus as if He were another Fire of Time (Kālānala), with His circle of arms drawing a bow drawn back to the ear on the field of battle— [The enemy shall perish.]

Having thus meditated upon Rāvaṇa— who is destroying all his enemies with showers of sharp weapons along the great path, who stands upon the chariot-road of the great heroic Indra, who is joined by Lakṣmaṇa and other great heroes such as Mada and others,

and who is pursued by tens of millions of great heroes holding mountains and trees in their hands, roaring with forceful, terrible *huṃkāras*, *bhobhos*, and great shouts while rushing toward him in battle— the best of practitioners, remaining without food, should again perform the offering for the sake of slaying the enemy with *śālmalī* flowers ten times [the number of mantras recited].

Even one enriched with sovereign power has no enemy remaining; having meditated upon the enemy Rāvaṇa and having made oneself the scion of Raghu (Rāma), one should destroy everything as before without effort. By that very means, he who was born of anger goes indeed to the abode of Yama. One who is utterly deprived of consciousness due to the grief of Sītā’s abduction should recite [the mantra] while meditating on the Lord of the Raghus, dwelling in water and subsisting on water. With a fire-oblation (*homa*) of sesame seeds ten times the number [of recitations], one should paralyze the host of enemies. Having placed the name [of the enemy] at the end of the seed-syllable of Vāyu (*yaṃ*), one should cause it to revolve.

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while fasting and also offer oblations of sesame seeds. Meditating upon Rāma as Viṣṇu, intent on searching for Sītā, one should mentally cause even an enemy—who is like a golden mountain—to wander for a long time.

One should meditate upon Rāma together with Lakṣmaṇa on the shore of the ocean near Laṅkā, in the vicinity of the golden ramparts, being worshipped by Sugrīva and other gods such as Jīvavān and others in their assembly. Then, one should recite the mantra for the sake of granting a boon to Vibhīṣaṇa, who has come seeking refuge and is pleased by him.

One should offer oblations with lotuses (*paṅkaja*) and quickly bring the king or the lord under one's control. Closing one’s eyes out of affection and perceiving [the deity] again and again, while gladdening the beloved of Maithilī, Rāma—the delighter of diversion—one should meditate upon him and recite the mantra a hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*), offering red lotuses as well; thus one swiftly deludes the king or the lord. Closing one’s eyes out of affection and perceiving [him] again and again, [one attains] the sixfold [powers], which are here irresistible and exceedingly sharp.

The demonstration of the ritual application (*prayoga*) is for the purpose of illuminating the reality of all desired objects; however, the statement that "it need not be performed again" is far removed from the truth. Furthermore, for those who perform rituals, there is no other world (*paraloka*); for them, the fruit will be nothing other than what lies within the scope of the ritual itself. For people free from desire, liberation (*mukti*) alone is the fruit resulting from recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), worship (*arcana*), and so forth; here, there is nothing else to be found. There is never a double fruit for any single injunction. (Sutīkṣṇa...)

Therefore, O wise one, one who is free from desire should worship Rāma. Having taken up the Brahmāstra mantra, one should not discharge it at rabbits and the like; this mantra does not bestow liberation and should not be employed for killing and such purposes. [Thus ends the fifteenth chapter of the Śrī Agasti Saṃhitā. Agastya said:

Now I shall describe the rules for the *puraścaraṇa* rite, without which there can be no success in a mantra even after hundreds of years. Devotion, faith, and the giving of gifts must be acquired over a long period.

Having received the excellent mantra from a well-pleased Guru—one which bestows all desired objects—one should daily worship as before and perform recitation (*japa*) with fixed vows, being pure, six thousand times, or one thousand, or one hundred and eight times. When Rāma, thus propitiated, awakens one's devotion, then the preliminary service (*pūrva-sevā*) is prescribed for the sake of the *puraścaraṇa* rite.

Restraining oneself according to one’s capacity, the knower of the Self should, like the *puraścaraṇa*, perform everything except the fire-oblation (*homa*). Then, one should make a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).

One who is self-controlled and firm in their vows should, with constant and uninterrupted devotion, perform this practice for a long time. It is recommended to be done on a mountain peak, in the midst of water, or on the shore of the saltless ocean; at the foot of an *aśvattha* tree on a riverbank, in a beautiful grove of *bilva* trees, in a shrine facing west where no bulls or such animals are present; in a forest of *aśvattha*, *bilva*, or *tulasī* trees, or amidst various flowers;
in cow-pens, at sacred fords (*tīrthas*), or in holy fields. This is praised for those who are pure, prosperous, virtuous, established in noble lineages, and endowed with Vedic conduct.

A twice-born man who subsists on alms should eat only what has been offered as an oblation (haviṣpātta), or vegetables, barley-gruel (yāvaka), fruits, roots, or even milk, whatever may be available there.

Having spread out [the base], poured [libations] over it, prepared it, and purified it with Vedic mantras such as the *prokṣaṇa* and others, the knower of mantras should again [consecrate it] with a mantra. He should perform the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) duties prescribed for his stage of life (*āśrama*), but he should avoid optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) and anything not ordained for his own stage of life. [He should also avoid] salt, sugar, alkaline substances, honey, other liquids, and black gram (*māṣa*).

One should avoid mung beans, lentils, and the like, as well as *kodrava* and chickpeas; one should also avoid conversation with others and the worship of other deities. With the mind fixed on that alone and devoted to it, one should perform that very rite while sleeping on the ground, being pure in soul, having conquered anger, and having subdued the senses. One should completely avoid speaking untruths and crooked speech. Even among those present at the assembly, one should not speak during the recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), worship, and so forth. If the practitioner must speak at that time, he should do so only when prompted by those in the assembly. Otherwise, everything performed will be entirely fruitless, even if it is done with satisfaction.

Free from desire for women and the like through speech, mind, and actions, he should avoid seeing or hearing songs, dances, and so forth, as well as betel, perfumes, ointments, and the wearing of flowers.

He should also avoid sexual intercourse, talk about it, and social gatherings concerning it. He should avoid crookedness, milk, oil massage, eating food that has not been offered, and actions performed without a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), as well as rubbing the body and similar acts. He should abandon bathing with hot water and using fragrant *āmalaka* and other such substances. He should purify his head internally and externally with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and he should bathe with *pañcagavya* alone.

Or one may bathe with *lāmalaka* (myrobalan) while reciting mantras declared in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas; thereafter, one should perform that which is to be practiced: food that is pure, most excellent, and constant; white rice, or winter rice, or *śāli* rice prepared from one's own stores; grain not threshed by a Śūdra, nor trodden by feet, nor struck by one other than a cow; curd, milk, ghee, and sugar-cane products, excluding jaggery; white sesame seeds, mung beans, and tubers—excluding *kemukas*; coconut fruit, plantain, *lavalī*, mango, myrobalan, jackfruit, *ādra*, and *harītakī*; these are praised for other vows as well.

The wise consider that which is not Vaiṣṇava to be unrefined and unfit for praise among other vows; if one desires one's own success, all such things must be abandoned here. When one of firm intellect has undertaken this Vaiṣṇava rite, being established in the resolve of forgiveness, non-violence, and compassion, one should daily and with self-restraint recite the mantra of Puruṣottama at the three junctions of the day. One should worship without distraction and first chant six hundred thousand times. Then, according to the prescribed rule, one should offer libations (tarpaṇa) with pure water containing flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings, ten parts of which have been purified by conduct. One should complete the full number of recitations.

Then, as before, having invoked Rāma into the sacrificial fire with bilva fruits, flowers, and even leaves, and having worshipped Him according to the previous rites, one should oneself perform the oblation (*homa*) using the three sweets (*madhuratraya*), or with leaves, or with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), or with sesame seeds—whichever of these is available. Thereafter, one should feed the Brahmins. Worship performed at the three junctions of the day, daily recitation (*japa*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), the fire-oblation, and the feeding of Brahmins—this is declared to be the *puraścaraṇa*. Once a mantra has been received from a guru and [the disciple] is satisfied, this five-fold worship (*pañcāṅgopāsana*) is prescribed as the preliminary to its accomplishment (*siddhi*). Thus it is ordained.

For those without desire, direct realization may indeed occur through this alone; for those with desire, the accomplishment of their aims occurs, but for all others, it would be entirely fruitless. The wise person who performs this five-limbed *puraścaraṇa* conquers the entire world through knowledge, sovereignty, sons, and other blessings. He himself becomes a donor, an enjoyer, and most excellent among beings in his various births. He becomes an expounder of the scriptures he has heard, one whose own learning is renowned upon the earth, long-lived, fortunate, possessed of sons and grandsons, auspicious, and highly intelligent. This very procedure shall be the glory of his righteousness.

O ascetic, whatever prosperity one desires, one may obtain that through the mind alone—even that which is unattainable for the gods, or that which is located in another continent. By performing the five-limbed worship (*pañcāṅgopāsana*), one shall attain whatever is desired. At the beginning, the end, and in the middle, one should feed many Brahmins day after day according to one's ability, out of devotion, with the garden (*rāma*) in view.

This five-limbed worship performed with devotion is called *puraścaraṇa*. O best among the learned, this is the cause of the destruction of saṃsāra; there is no dharma equal to this, and there is no austerity equal to this.

O ascetic, there is nothing equal to this for the attainment of one's desired goal, whether it be a fire-sacrifice (*homa*), worship, or libation (*tarpaṇa*). O noble ones, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) may be accomplished by two parts alone: by recitation (*japa*) of that same number and by the propitiation of Brahmins. If any part [of the rite] is omitted, a recitation twice that number must be performed out of devotion by one who is unable to complete it, so that the rite may be perfected with all its limbs. If no limb is omitted, then one shall obtain the desired fruit. Whatever rite is performed deficient in its limbs cannot accomplish the desired goal; therefore, one must by all means feed Brahmins to ensure the completeness of the rite.

For the sake of accomplishment, by the mere act of honoring a Brahmin, one who is deficient in limbs attains completeness; likewise, rites performed with omissions or excesses do not fulfill one's desires. However, if they are honored with that [gift], all rites bear fruit. Therefore, in all rituals, one should diligently feed the learned. Whatever rites are deprived of the feeding of twice-born men become as useless on this earth as seeds without sprouts. Among the hundreds of thousands of praises for him, external worship is commended. The mantra for the propitiation of Rāma is supreme when accompanied by meditation and recitation.

This very *Maṃtrārthalocanā* is the self-evident achiever of one's desired goal; he who constantly worships Rāma with flowers should contemplate Him within those very flowers. For him, there shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation in this life—of this there is no doubt. (51) [Thus ends the sixteenth chapter of the *Śrī Agastisaṃhitā*. Agastya said: Now I shall describe the unsurpassed procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā-vidhi*) and the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), without which one does not achieve success even through hundreds of practices. A practitioner of pure soul should diligently please the Guru by means of wealth, mental devotion, and desires.
Endowed with devotion and faith, as the preceptor himself gives with contentment and a cheerful countenance, so indeed should the disciple follow the prescribed procedure.

O Sage, at a pure time and place, the pure-souled and self-restrained Guru, having performed the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), should perform the sowing of the sprouts; he should first perform the *nāndīmukha* śrāddha and the recitation of auspicious blessings (*svastivācana*) according to the rules prescribed in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. If this is done in the month of Madhu (Caitra), there will be sorrow; in Mādhava (Vaiśākha), an accumulation of jewels; and in Jyeṣṭha, death occurs.

In the month of Śrāvaṇa, there will certainly be the destruction of kinsmen; in Bhādrapada, there will surely be the decline of subjects. In the month of Āśvina, however, everything is indeed auspicious.

In Kārtika, there shall be knowledge, and in Mārgaśīrṣa, happiness also occurs. In Pauṣa, there is a loss of knowledge, while in Māgha, there is an increase in intelligence. In Phālguna as well, there will be prosperity; one should avoid the intercalary month (Malamāsa). Under the Sun, Jupiter, Venus, the Moon, Mercury, or Saturn; and in the constellations of Aśvinī, Revatī, Svātī, Viśākhā, Hasta, the three Jyeṣṭhās, and the three Uttarās—one should thus perform the consecration with mantras on a full-moon day.

The fifth, second, seventh, thirteenth, and tenth lunar days are praised as bestowing all desired fruits. On a day pure in its five limbs (pacāṅga-śuddha), when there is the rising of the sun, the lunar day, and the weekday; when Jupiter and Venus are rising, the ascendant is pure, and the twelfth house is cleared; and when the moon and stars are favorable—it is commended for all rites. There is nothing equal to the time of a solar eclipse; whatever is performed therein becomes infinitely fruitful. O Lord of Sages, on the occasion of a solar parvan, there is no need for the purification of the lunar day or the weekday; whatever desired house one gives at that time [is efficacious].

The mantra attains success quickly and without effort; therefore, those desiring the perfection of the mantra should, with every effort, perform the ritual ablution of Rāma’s mantra at that very place.

Having properly constructed a maṇḍala there using four colors—blue, yellow, white, and black—as before, and having placed two handfuls of grain upon it, one should worship Hari there, having filled a jar with water from sacred fords (tīrtha) accompanied by a coconut fruit, radiant all around with auspicious items, and attended by every festival, while reciting the hymns (sūkta) of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as the Smārta rites.

One should worship the Lord with both Puranic mantras and Vaishnava Agamic mantras. One should honor the Brahmins with garments, earrings, and finger-rings, and cause them to recite their own hymns (*sūkta*) and the mantras of Viṣṇu, O Sage. The preceptor should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth according to the previously mentioned rules; having performed the array of ritual placements (*nyāsa*), he should worship there as before.

Puruṣottama is to be worshipped with the aforementioned materials, and one should conduct the festival there with the previously mentioned songs, dances, and other festivities. One should give in great abundance to virtuous women and householders.

O storehouse of asceticism, one should offer perfumes, flowers, water, betel, fine garments, ornaments, and so forth, as well as food and drink to others; having thus celebrated the festival there, one should perform the night vigil. In this manner, one should worship the Lord three times a day, both by day and by night. O Sage, one should recite the mantra six thousand times there at the conclusion of the worship day and night. On the following day, likewise in the morning, one should perform everything as before. Having worshipped Rāma according to the rules, one should perform the fire-ritual (agnikārya) as prescribed. One should prepare the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the mandala there as previously described, and having established the fire there, one should worship the Lord Rāma therein.

Having invoked [the deity] along with the limbs and the protective coverings according to the previous rules and as prescribed, one should perform everything starting from the installation of the fire as before. One should offer oblations of sesame seeds mixed with curd, milk, and clarified butter in ten parts (daśāṃśa).

Having performed the homa and offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should worship the pitcher situated there. Then, having offered the bali-offering in the cardinal directions, one should carry out what has been prescribed. Then, having brought the disciple—who is free from sin and bowed with devotion—near, and having performed breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) according to the rules, one should, together with many Brahmins, sprinkle him on the head with that water from the pitcher while reciting the mantra "surāstvām... (The gods [protect] you...).

"Nārāyaṇa himself as Rāma shall surely bestow his presence upon the disciple; he who is all-pervading and hidden everywhere, the ocean of mercy, is pleased. Having thus consecrated [the disciple] and remembering this, one should sprinkle him with those waters.

Then, having dressed him in garments, anointed him with sandalwood paste and the like, and caused him to wear earrings and a ring, one should thereafter perform the Vaiṣṇava Mātṛkā-nyāsa, the Tattva-nyāsa, the Mūrti-pañjara-nyāsa, and the Ṛṣyādi-nyāsa, duly placing them upon the body of the disciple according to the previous rules. Then, placing one's own hand upon his head, one should recite [the mantra] a hundred times.

O bull among sages, having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times, the Guru should diligently bestow it upon that disciple preceded by the offering of water. The Guru should meditate on the knowledge (*vidyā*), consisting of light, as departing from himself; the disciple should meditate on it as having arrived, thinking especially, "I am blessed. Then, having accomplished his purpose, the disciple, with a joyful mind, should offer everything to the Guru according to his devotion—cows, land, gold, forests, houses, fields, and so forth, O Sage. If he cannot give all, he should give half, or a quarter, or even a twelfth part; or else, without causing hardship, he should give food, clothing, and wealth according to his means.

In essence, adopting another method, one should diligently please the guru; one should personally please the guru’s sons, wife, and others with many offerings, such as worship, along with garments and ornaments, out of devotion. Having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the guru in the manner described, and considering oneself to have fulfilled one's duty, one should feed the Brahmins and give them sacrificial fees as well, satisfying them all. Strengthened by the words of the Brahmin women and the guru’s blessings, the knower of mantras should dismiss the guru and the others, and then eat. Thus, the mantra is obtained without obstacle.

For one who has accomplished his purpose, there is no doubt regarding food; however, he should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*) with self-restraint by the command of his guru. At evening, morning, and midday, having meditated, he should mutter the mantra. Having purified the water with the mantra and veiled it with the *kavaca* (armor) mantra, the knower of mantras should properly form a circle in the water with the root of a *darbha* blade. Having invoked the sacred bathing-place (*tīrtha*) with the mudrās of invocation and so forth, he should worship it with this prayer: "O Sun, by that truth through which the sacred bathing-places within the cosmic egg were created by your rays, grant me the divine bathing-place, O Maker of Day! O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī!"

"O Sage, establish yourself within this water of truth; having thus worshipped and invoked [the deity] according to the rules, take that water properly in your cupped hands (añjali) and mutter the Mālā-mantra once.

Then, pour the water held in the right hand into the left hand. Thereafter, being self-restrained, one should mutter the Gāyatrī mantra: 'rāmo'hamasmi' (I am Rāma). Whatever sin has been accumulated since birth, whether by ten, a hundred, or even a thousand repetitions, or whatever was committed in the past—having uttered the word 'Daśarathāya', then the word 'vidmahe', and then raising the word 'Sītā', followed by 'vallabhāyai'..."
"Let us meditate upon that [Dhīmahī], and may He also impel [us] (pracodayāt). This is the Gāyatrī of Rāma, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Its *puraścaraṇa* consists of a recitation (*japa*) of four hundred thousand times; one should perform all other rites, such as worship, exactly as previously described. This Gāyatrī beginning with "Oṃ" grants liberation alone. That beginning with "Māyā" (Hrīṃ) grants scholarship, O Sage, and that beginning with "Ramā" (Śrīṃ) grants prosperity. Even when joined with "Madana" (Klīṃ), it infatuates the entire earth. When worshipped with this mantra, Rāma grants every desired object.

Then, O Lord of Sages, one should satisfy [the deity] preceded by the recitation of the root mantra, while praising and bowing with devotion according to one's capacity. Having performed this correctly every day at the three junctions of the day according to the prescribed rule, the practitioner of the mantra becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose; this is the truth, the absolute truth, and not otherwise. (62) [Thus ends the seventeenth chapter of the Agastya-saṃhitā.]

Agastya said: Now we shall also describe the characteristics of the various modes of worship. O Lord of Sages, water, sandalwood paste, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and the like are the primary materials for worship. Regarding their vessels, even large ones, the conch shell is also prescribed as a suitable vessel. A golden pitcher—or one made of other precious metals—that is not previously offered by another, is pure, naturally beautiful, and very cool, is desired as a vessel for worship. [The flowers] should be unoffered by others, fragrant, white, yellow, or otherwise pleasing to the mind, and free from holes.

In this matter, they praise even flowers that are devoid of fragrance; otherwise, everything would be useless. Sandalwood produced on the Malaya mountains, though naturally cool, is not as effective if it has not been smelled [before]. Incense made from camphor, aguru, and musk, or scented with snow and other substances, is commended for worship when placed in a vessel made of copper, bronze, or similar materials. O Sage, when the vessel is shaped like a lotus with a stalk attached to its base, and when incense derived from guggulu and aguru trees, or from resins and the finest fragrant substances, is cast into the fire, this offering of scent—unshared by others—is highly praised in the act of worship.

O Sage, a lamp—prepared as before in a vessel, shaped like a mandala, lit with a wick soaked in cow’s ghee, clarified butter, or other such substances, and offered by no one else—is highly commended for the rite of worship.

O Sage, the food offering (*naivedya*) intended for Hari should be prepared with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), flowers, and fruits; it should be pure, endowed with the six tastes, and offered by no one else. For the worship of the virtuous, the betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*) is also offered.
The site should be a sacred grove, a forest, or a riverbank; it should be level, four cubits square, with a well-constructed altar one cubit high, and adorned with moon-lights, banners, and the like.

A place that is pure and especially secluded is recommended for the rite of worship. Vessels made of copper, gold, and other materials, as well as lotuses fashioned from water, are highly commended for the presentation of water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings during worship. Pure ritual services (*upacāra*) are particularly praised therein. A conch shell named *samāvarta*, which has a whorl in its center and a smooth interior, when filled with white water, is recommended for the rite of worship. These and many other implements for worship exist; they are classified as superior, middling, or inferior.

One who is wealthy and capable should perform [the worship] with the most excellent materials; one of middling means, with middling materials; and one of lesser means, with inferior materials, O ascetic. Even if one is capable, if one has fallen into distress, one should perform it with even fewer materials.

According to the specific requirements of the ritual of worship, in accordance with place and time, according to one's power, and according to what is proper, one should act so as not to be censured by the world. Or, some may perform the entire worship of the deity in secret. Afterward, one should display the mudrās which cause the presence of the deity; when displayed, they delight the gods.

O Sage Sutīkṣṇa, these mudrās are to be shown by you during the ritual of the deity’s sacrifice: the Āvāhanī (invoking), Sthāpanī (establishing), Sānnidhyakāriṇī (bringing into presence), Susannirodhinī (firmly restraining), Sammukhīkaraṇī (facing toward), Sakalīkaraṇa (the rite of integration), and likewise the Mahāmudrā; as well as the conch, discus, mace, lotus, bow, Kaustubha gem, Garuḍa, Śrīvatsa, forest garland, and the Yoni-mudrā. Then, having brought the handful of flowers from the Mūlādhāra to the end of the twelve [finger-breadths], one should direct it toward the image and other objects through the splendors residing in the three places.

O Sage, this very mudrā is for the invocation (āvāhanīya) in the rite of deity worship; it is also considered the mudrā for its [the deity's] complete withdrawal (saṃnirodhinī). When the two fists are turned upward and brought face-to-face, it is regarded as the sammukhīkariṇī. The arrangement of the other limbs constitutes the sakalīkaraṇa. With both hands spread out and the thumbs joined to one another, this is called the Mahāmudrā, which brings about the completion of what is deficient or redundant. With the little fingers, ring fingers, middle fingers, and index fingers of both hands folded into a bud-like shape, this mudrā is known as the Śaṅkha, used in the worship of the gods. Another...

With the fingers facing each other, the middle fingers raised, and the two thumbs placed between them, O ascetic, the complete circular formation of the fingers constitutes the *padmamudrā*. Following that is the *dhenumudrā*. Then, with the ring fingers and little fingers joined to one another, and the index and middle fingers likewise joined face-to-face, it is known as the *kaustubhamudrā*. Furthermore, when the little fingers are joined to one another and facing each other, and the left index finger is placed between the middle and ring fingers, and [the right] touches the left ring finger...
The thumb and index finger placed on the middle finger, alternating; the two thumbs characterized as the *kaustubha*;

the little fingers joined together and crossed, brought down from above onto the thumbs—this is the mudrā known as Garuḍa. Then, the index and thumbs situated upon the middle finger, with the pair of middle and ring fingers, and the two hands with the little, ring, middle, and tips of the index fingers joined—O Sage, this is the Śrīvatsa mudrā. Following that, the fist formed by the little, ring, and middle fingers, with the index finger raised and whirled high above the head, constitutes the Vanamālā mudrā.

O Sage, the *mudrā* known as *yoni* is described as being formed by both hands joined together; when the two index fingers are drawn toward the middle fingers, followed by the pair of ring fingers, and the thumb is placed at the base of the middle fingers—this is to be known as the *śāstrārcana-mudrā*. Whoever constantly worships Rāma with these ten *mudrās* and the seven previously mentioned ones shall delight the Lord of the Gods, subdue even the king of serpents, and thereafter obtain his every prayer. O best of sages, I shall now describe the characteristics of the seats (*āsanas*); may they be auspicious.

When the feet are placed with the soles turned upward and the knees and thighs are held steady and even, this is called the Vīrāsana; it is declared to be the best among all postures. When the heel is placed on the opposite thigh and the other foot is positioned between the thighs, this is known as the Yogāsana, which grants the desires of the yogi. Furthermore, when one places the heels against the sides of the opposite thighs and brings the two knees together evenly, this becomes the Gomukhāsana.

It destroys the flood of all sins; there are many types of seats. In this very way, during recitations (*japa*) and other rites, whatever seat the wise man finds, having sat upon it, he should perform the recitations and so forth, endowed with devotion, and meditate upon Puruṣottama. O Sage, he who performs worship, recitation, fire-offerings (*homa*), and so on in this manner, becomes worthy of honor by all in this world and the next. Worship, recitation, fire-offerings, and likewise the oblation (*āhuti*) of mantras, as well as the path of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*abhiṣeka*), have been shown to you, O one whose wealth is austerity. O observer of good vows, the characteristics of the articles for worship and the like have also been shown.

Without effort, grasp with all devotion that which was spoken by Sutīkṣṇa—the Vaiṣṇava mantra which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. It is my conviction that this must not be told to those who are not Vaiṣṇavas, nor should it be heard by them; however, it should indeed be given with effort to a devotee of Viṣṇu who requests it. (56) [Thus ends the eighteenth chapter of the Śrī Agastisaṃhitā. Agastya said: Among the excellent mantras of Sutīkṣṇa, the Vaiṣṇava is said to be the best. It grants desires among the Gāṇapatya, Śaiva, Śākta, and Saura mantras; and even among all the Vaiṣṇava mantras, the fruit of the Rāma-mantra is supreme.

Fie upon the mantras of the Gaṇapatyas and others! This six-syllabled mantra (Ṣaḍakṣara) is superior to them by millions upon millions of times; among them all, this six-syllabled mantra bestows fruit without effort. This six-syllabled mantra is the destroyer of the entire flood of sins; it is proclaimed as the king of mantras, the most excellent of all. It burns away daily misfortune, as well as that born of fortnights, months, seasons, and years, leaving nothing behind, just as fire consumes a mountain of cotton. Thousands of killings of Brahmins, whether committed knowingly or unknowingly, tens of thousands of thefts of gold, drinking of liquor, and violations of the Guru’s bed—even millions [of such sins]—[it destroys].

Even thousands of millions of minor offenses (*upapātaka*) all go to destruction together through the recitation of Rāma’s mantra. Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, kūṣmāṇḍas, grahas, and rākṣasas flee from afar by the power of Rāma’s mantra. Whatever impurity, confusion, or defilement there may be, it all reaches dissolution when Rāma’s mantra is recited.

Even the defects of the seed (*bīja-doṣa*) up to the level of Brahmā, as well as those arising from the violation of observances (*niyama*), whether belonging to women or men, are destroyed by this mantra. In whatever regions [these occur]...

Rāma is worshipped supremely by others out of fear of famine and such calamities, but he is never otherwise; he is peaceful, gracious, a granter of boons, free from anger, and affectionate toward his devotees. There is no mantra equal to this, even for one who is merely reciting it. When Rāma is propitiated with this, he becomes truly pleased at once; he bestows prosperity, sovereignty, and even equality with or superiority over the gods. By the mere utterance of this, one intent on the worship of the mantra attains all desires through enjoyment, and if desireless, liberation itself. Furthermore, one who desires freedom from fear attains both enjoyment and liberation; of this there is no doubt.

Sutīkṣṇa said: "O best among those who possess the knowledge that determines the meaning of the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas, please sever my doubt; I ask you, grant me your grace. The wise who know the truth of the Śruti and other scriptures declare: 'One indeed attains the eternal Brahman, which is free from rebirth, through direct realization in the form of self-experience. O venerable one, explain how those devoted to the practice of mantras attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation, as described by you. Furthermore, cessation is called liberation (mukti), while engagement is called worldly enjoyment (bhukti); [please explain] the nature of both."

"Tell me, O best of speakers, how the path may be; tell me that which was spoken by you, for it is the truth, the absolute truth. Liberation is defined as cessation—the cessation of all worldly happiness and the cessation of suffering in reality—and it is characterized by withdrawal. In this world, they declare that 'enjoyment' consists of the complete engagement of the senses with objects along with the heart; yet here, there is a disparity between these two. Nevertheless, the contemplation of the Self is seen in both cases. For liberation is indeed the abiding of the Self through the contemplation of the Self. This is certainly so for those who know the truth and understand all principles."

The virtuous, who experience the Self at all times, whether engaged in worldly activity or withdrawn from it, always pursue only Rāma, thinking, "This is indeed Māyā. They are certainly not transmigrating beings; of this there is no doubt.

Here, Rāma alone is the enjoyer, while the noble act of eating is the object of enjoyment. Since the one [Rāma] alone remains as the perfected one, what room is there for the association with the unreal? Therefore, enjoyment is not held to be an obstacle to the path of liberation. By this method, he who practices toward Rāma attains both enjoyment and liberation; of this there is no doubt. Just as...

One should avoid both praise and censure, as well as those who approach [the devotee] for the sake of worldly gain; likewise, one should not touch such people. A follower of Rāma, with a mind focused on no other, should always contemplate, "I am indeed Rāma. For such a person, there is nothing in the world that is prescribed nor anything that is forbidden. Therefore, those who speak with the intent, "I am indeed Rāma," have their every prescribed duty fulfilled by the name of Rāma alone. Whatever they give to him day after day—be it water, food, or clothing—it is given to Rāma himself; of this there is no doubt. Thus, whatever is given to the knower of Brahman is given to Rāma.

Even those who hate or revile him are destined for infinity; they become vessels for the fruits of that sin and will undoubtedly be impoverished householders, filled with suffering. Furthermore, after producing a son, he himself might even burn him; he is imprisoned in all jails without cause. Alas! For one of such meager fortune, this state shall continue until his destruction. Therefore, those who desire the fruit [of liberation] should not harbor hatred toward the knowers of Brahman, nor should they ever engage in reviling them; rather, they should act only for their benefit. Those who praise, rejoice in, or give to him—[to such a person...]

Those who have attained that merit obtain its entirety once they have known Him as their very Self; therefore, perform your duty continuously with this understanding. By this alone, all your desires will be fulfilled, and not otherwise. Abandon the company of those who hold such views and the desire for worldly diversion; practice what is beneficial. Always remain among the virtuous and be supremely devoted to non-violence (*ahiṃsā*). There are eight means for attaining that [Self]; I shall describe them, so listen: restraint (*yama*), the one called observance (*niyama*), and posture (*āsana*) as the third; breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) shall be the fourth, while withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) is the fifth; concentration (*dhāraṇā*)...
O observer of good vows, I shall now describe the characteristics of each of these [virtues] one by one; indeed, I shall explain their respective definitions in detail.

Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, straightforwardness, forbearance, fortitude, moderation in diet, and purity—these are known as the ten *yamas*. Furthermore, not causing distress to any living beings through speech, mind, or action is truly defined as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*). O ascetic, the non-appropriation of another's property, even so much as a blade of grass, is this which is called non-stealing (*asteya*).

Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is declared to be the eternal means for attaining Brahman; it consists of the total renunciation of association with women through deed, mind, and speech, even in all circumstances.

Compassion (*dayā*) is described by the wise as the contemplation of the suffering of others after having reflected upon one's own, followed by the pursuit of the means to alleviate it. Integrity (*ārjava*) is the absence of crookedness in all dealings whatsoever, through the actions of mind, speech, and body toward everyone. And selflessness (*anātmabhāva*) is the state of being entirely free from the sense of "mine" at all times and in every place, even toward those who cause harm.

O best of sages, forbearance is conduct toward one's kinsmen; the wise declare that steadfastness is the absence of desire and effort even regarding objects already acquired, like one free from greed—O best of the virtuous.

Eating only a fourth part of what is fit for consumption, with a mind [controlled], avoiding excessively pungent, bitter, sour, and salty foods, and consuming what is wholesome, pure, and well-digested—that is called right diet; otherwise, it is declared to be wrong diet. They say that impurity is what has emerged from the pores of the skin and the various openings; the cleansing of these gates is called purification through earth and water.

The wise declare that external purification (*śauca*) consists of the thorough cleansing of the body with earth and water, followed by the previously mentioned purification of the elements (*bhūta-śuddhi*). These ten restraints (*yama*), O Brahmin, are the means for attaining that Brahman:

austerity (*tapas*), contentment (*tuṣṭi*), faith (*āstikya*), worship of the Lord (*īśvarārādhana*), study of the established doctrines (*siddhāntāvekṣaṇa*), modesty (*lajjā*), generosity (*dāna*), intellect (*mati*), recitation (*japa*), and vows (*vrata*). These ten are known as the sharp observances (*niyama*). O ascetic, I shall describe the characteristics of each one of these. Austerity (*tapas*) is intended to be fasting according to the prescribed rules.

One who lives for the sake of satisfaction through fasting without effort—this is what contentment is understood to be; its attainment does not occur without the Śruti. When joined with practice (*yukta*), it is proclaimed as faith and steadfastness (*āstikya*). The proper worship of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) daily according to the rules at the three junctions of the day, or even once, constitutes the worship of the Lord (*Īśvara*). Likewise, there is the hearing and reflection upon the established conclusions (*siddhānta*) of the Vaiṣṇava Āgamas. At midday, one should gaze upon the sun while listening to the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and so forth. Indeed, this is called "listening to the established conclusion."

That which is utterly condemned by those who perceive the truth through the Vedas and other scriptures, as well as by worldly people—refraining from that is the practice for one possessed of shame. Furthermore, having meditated upon one's chosen deity, whatever is offered daily into the sacrificial vessel with the thought of it being an offering to Him is called *dhyāna*. The constant repetition of the mantra received from the Guru, preceded by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the internal syllables, constitutes *japa*. The undertaking of all prescribed observances is *vrata*; everything apart from these observances is [the path of] action.

Whatever is performed with *yamas* and *niyamas* shall become fruitful; therefore, through *niyama*, everything performed attains success. (65) [Thus ends the nineteenth chapter of the Śrī Agastisaṃhitā. (19) Agastya said: Remaining in one place alone along with the previously mentioned *niyamas*—this is not called the posture (*āsana*) for one whose body is fixed upon a stake. Now I shall describe the *prāṇāyāmas* which are beneficial to the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), by which, when practiced, the flood of sins is burnt away like a mountain of dry fuel. Even the defects arising from wind, bile, and phlegm, as well as those produced from the skin, blood, flesh, fat, marrow, bones, and semen—all these are consumed by the restraint of the breath within the body. Indeed, they declare this to be the primary atonement for the multitude of sins for those desiring the eternal Brahman, which is free from rebirth. Furthermore, O Sage, *prāṇāyāma* must be performed constantly according to the rules; having properly restrained the vital breaths and the internal organ within the Self, one remains alone and attains the state of Brahman.

One should snap the fingers once after quickly touching the knees three times with the tips of the hands; this is considered the shortest measure (*mātrā*). The medium is double that, and the longest is considered triple.

The lowest, medium, and highest forms of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) are as follows: the lowest is held for fifteen measures, the medium for thirty, and the highest is said to be forty-five measures. O Sage, by constantly performing sixteen such breath controls every day, all daily sin is certainly destroyed.

The sin born of harming others, the sin born of seizing another’s property, and that produced by sexual union with another’s wife—all these are consumed by a hundred *prāṇāyāmas*. Even all the hundreds of killings of Brahmins arising from the category of great sins (*mahāpātaka*) perish through four hundred *prāṇāyāmas*. One should diligently perform *prāṇāyāmas* at the beginning and at the end of all ritual acts, whether they be auspicious or inauspicious. Whatever action is performed without *prāṇāyāmas* is fruitless; therefore, those who desire welfare should diligently perform *prāṇāyāmas* as much as possible according to their capacity.

Restraining the vital breaths with the mind alone, the wise man should mutter the mantra while meditating repeatedly on Rāma, Rāma, according to the previously described rule. Holding the breath within and closing his eyes slightly, he should meditate upon the Supreme Light within and mutter the mantra. Just as fire completely penetrates from the feet to the head, so too should the restraint of the breath be measured by the same number of *mātrās* by which the body is agitated when it runs after the objects of the senses. Any ritual action such as recitation (*japa*) or burnt offerings (*homa*) performed without breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is [ineffective]. The sky...

All these [six limbs] should indeed be practiced with effort. The withdrawal of the senses from their objects, even when they have been drawn toward them, is *pratyāhāra*; this constitutes the complete restraint of the senses. Or, the confinement of the individual soul (*jīva*) within the form of Brahman through various methods—arising from the three-fold *prāṇāyāma* described previously—is *dhāraṇā*, which is the stabilization of the mind upon the Self. *Dhyāna* is right contemplation; having placed Rāma in the heart, together with His limbs and ornaments, as well as His invocation and acts of descent, it is the realization of Truth and Knowledge.

Samādhi is the means for attaining oneness with bliss; it consists of reflecting upon the Dharma even in other states of existence, or else it is the contemplation of the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman. Having become one with Brahman, the individual soul itself remains as its own essence alone—the state where the vital breaths are restrained and the elements have dissolved, being non-different from the Reality that exists. Furthermore, samādhi is said to be even that which lasts for a mere moment. Thus, one who is endowed with the eight limbs, disciplined in yoga, and well-restrained, having pierced the orb of the sun, goes to the eternal Brahman. He who practices thus constantly, free from fear, [attains the goal].

One who is peaceful, whose collection of senses has been brought under control, who has cast off all evil, and who is free from desire and anger, is fit for immortality. Thus, through the yoga of practice, the yogi attains the supreme goal. Whether by the yoga of action, the yoga of knowledge, or by both, the eternal Brahman, which is free from rebirth, is attained. He who daily performs actions consisting of recitation and fire-offerings while casting away the desire for their respective fruits—be it with attributes (saguṇa) or without attributes (nirguṇa)—and meditates upon the descendant of Raghu, [attains that same state].

Through the knowledge of equanimity, one indeed attains the supreme state; and he who practices yoga daily through meditation and action surely reaches the highest station, from which having gone, one does not return.

Therefore, O storehouse of asceticism, with very sharp effort, through vows, fasts, and observances performed for ten million births, and through various sacrifices, devotion to Rāghava arises perfectly. You are the boat for reaching the further shore of this ocean of saṃsāra. Whether you are a practitioner of karma-yoga or enter into jñāna-yoga, do so quickly for all beings who are wandering among living creatures.

Rāghava himself is indeed the sole protector for those whose minds have strayed into saṃsāra. For those whose every sin has been utterly exhausted, the yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga) is praised; however, the yoga of action (karmayoga) is the means to liberation for all. One should worship Rāma properly here through either knowledge or action. That body of his is extremely sharp, subject to decay, and prone to falling; it is composed of skin, blood, flesh, marrow, bone, fat, and semen. They say that its proper purification is that which is established by the scriptures. [The yoga of action] is the means to the final goal, destroying [all obstacles]. The yoga of action...
O best of those who know Yoga, one might think, "I shall perform my duty," whether it be through worldly knowledge or Yoga; yet this fool would only be casting dust into his own eyes.

To one whose mind is firmly established in perfect dispassion (*vairāgya*) and fixed upon reality, all sense-objects appear of their own accord like vomited food. Dispassion shines only in one who has truly renounced the nature of the body along with its vital breaths. Even that [dispassion] must be swiftly abandoned by one who is dispassionate in every respect—[the realization that] even the final impurity residing within the body is worse than being situated in the midst of excrement. This is the truth.

One considers it especially beneficial for living beings; yet such impurity in this body of embodied ones is such that at the touch of even a single part, such as the skin, bathing itself is prescribed. Even by jackals and vultures it is carried away—oh, what a decree fate ordains! For the enemies of the body, the skin is not [enough] for embodied beings; rather, such is the state of its every step and position. Therefore, the person of deluded intellect remains attached to the body of the universe; this body was created by Fate solely for the purpose of experiencing misery. Even one who knows the ultimate truth perceives this...

Being deluded, one does not perceive this; in this world, it is by the very *māyā* of the Great Soul Viṣṇu that his body, having become manifest, deludes the entire universe. Having become composed of *māyā*, he wanders again and again within the whirlpool of suffering, distressed by the maintenance of a family. O one whose wealth is penance, he perceives only suffering and not happiness at all. That which brings misery to everyone must be renounced with one's whole being. What fool, already ruined, would enter [this path] again, ruined even from the start? Not even the slightest action here is fruitless.

O Sage, if that [bond] still exists, then even one who is liberated would be bound again upon re-entry; therefore, wise men should not perform actions out of a desire for results. If they were to perform them, the result would be that—provided they perform worship and other rites without such expectation—they do not fall into the whirlpool of suffering in saṃsāra, deluded as they may be; for even the Lord is able to rescue them, and not otherwise.
(Thus ends the twentieth chapter of the Śrī Agasti-saṃhitā. Agastya said: Now, O Sage, I shall proclaim that which is more secret than the secret. What...

O treasure of asceticism, listen to that which destroys suffering with what remains; one should also reflect that even action is a means for attaining that [liberation]. For it is indeed through actions alone that the secret of the virtuous and the good is ordained; how could that which is focused on a single point not lead to liberation from the unreal? Indeed, whatever person is enjoined to a specific qualification in this world, such a one does not exist [without following the path]; wealth obtained by righteous means is truly a treasure. Where would the officiating priests—who know the truth of the ritual and desire the welfare of the sacrificer—remain, as well as the mantras taught and restrained [in their application]?

Even if one has studied according to the rules, how can there be a correct recitation? How can such an action be accepted as a means for attaining a fruit? Whichever thing is enjoined as a means in this regard, if that very thing is rendered defective through negligence, then even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or Maheśvara cannot perform or cause it to be performed as a means. This is the understanding established by the ordinance itself. Who else, having performed the action according to the rules, could achieve the desired fruit? Both the performer of the action and the ritual injunction, along with the many required means—this is the [truth].

One should thoroughly emaciate [the body] through penances such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* according to the prescribed rules. If one is not overcome by these, then even if overcome, nothing—whether pleasant or unpleasant—will affect one's own self;

however, the most sinful person falls into hell. Thereafter, through the ripening of karma, having attained the state of trees, shrubs, creepers, and so forth, one attains the state of worms, insects, and other small creatures.
In this very manner, one revolves again and again like a wheel. Whatever action, whether prescribed or forbidden, one performs, one shall not escape from *saṃsāra*.

O Sage, at no time is there any other means for liberation than knowledge; it is true that you are established in knowledge, yet that [knowledge] arises only through yoga, and yoga is preceded by practice (*abhyāsa*). Practice, moreover, arises through the restraints (*yama*) and so forth, and not otherwise. These restraints and others are practiced by those who have studied the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras, who are detached, of a sattvic nature, and who have abandoned the conceit of "I" regarding the body. However, even the conceit of "I" regarding their own bodies persists in them only as long as they do not know the truth of the eternal and the non-eternal.

Even those who possess tranquility, for whom there is no other path than liberation, no other austerity than liberation, and no other meditation than liberation—there is nothing else beyond that. Having attained the state of a renunciant (*yatitva*), abandon even the sense of "mine" regarding the body and so forth, if you truly desire complete liberation. Know the Self perfectly and continuously;

when the body and such have thus departed, the Self alone remains by itself. Therefore, O one rich in penance, nothing exists that is higher than the Self. And this being so, even this suffering of saṃsāra exists [only in relation to it].

He whose intellect is deluded does not strive for the state of a *yati* (renunciant) apart from the practice of asceticism; yet, without such striving, even one who knows Brahman does not exist for the sake of ultimate liberation from suffering. The turning away from all sense-objects with one's whole being, when conjoined with the knowledge of Brahman, is the state of a *yati*, which is the means for realizing Brahman. In truth, there is no other means whatsoever for liberation. Therefore, that [knowledge] is the refuge of all, the source of all auspiciousness, and the bestower of all perfections. Just as the Bhagirathi Ganges, having met with the ocean, purifies those who have fallen into it, so too does the knowledge of Brahman purify all beings.

O Sage, he who is devoted to the practice of yoga purifies the three worlds merely by his sight, becoming the foremost among those who perfectly know Brahman; whereas even a twelve-year penance duly performed or the state of a renunciant (*yatitva*) properly undertaken purify only oneself quickly. Therefore, with one's whole being, one should constantly practice for the sake of the absolute liberation of Brahman. (43)

[Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the glorious Agasti-saṃhitā. (21) Sutīkṣṇa said: "O best among those who know Yoga, tell me what this 'Yoga' is; O Lord of Sages, by what means can the conquest of the mind be achieved? By what does one attain the taste of the essence of knowledge and bliss, from which one never turns back? You desire the steadiness of the mind without effort; therefore, [one should restrain] the apāna... Agastya said: "First, the vital breath (samīraṇa) within the body should be restrained; then the mind likewise is restrained. When it is thus restrained, it seeks union with the Self. From that, one does not turn back from the tasting of the flavor of knowledge and bliss. Therefore, you must expect the immobility of the mind without exertion. Then, the apāna..."

Having drawn up the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and raised them, one should join the *prāṇa* and *apāna* together; having made the mind also established in the Self, one should savor bliss—this is remembered as the rite of the "End of the Twelve" (*dvādaśānta*). One should never abandon that which is higher than this. First, know these to be the causes for the arising of the body, as well as the process of its non-falling once arisen, and the agent of the Self. Saṃsāra is indeed beginningless, yet it is seen that the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is the cause; according to that [cause], the procedure bestows grace in many ways through various most delicious [experiences].

O treasure of asceticism, although they are divided into various forms, the number of all these [beings] is infinite; thus the Śruti declares that there is no limit to their diversity within the Self. Because saṃsāra is beginningless, even for one who is a treasure of the arising of perfect knowledge, this much suffering alone is experienced here. The wise say that the seeds of these are born from eggs, born from sweat, and born from wombs; furthermore, they are manifold, fourfold, and otherwise in many ways. Then, having taken hold of the earth, they arise as those born from sprouts. These are the forms consisting of the five elements, such as grass and the like.

O storehouse of austerity, those [beings] there also undergo transformation through the differentiation of flowers, fruits, trunks, and branches; even those born from eggs remain undetermined in forms such as the *godhā* lizard and others, and other well-known beings born from sweat perish moment by moment in the form of lice, insects, and the like. Those born from a womb (*jarāyuja*) attain birth through the power of their own matured *adṛṣṭa* (latent merit/demerit) once it has been exhausted by experience. Through the sexual union of a man and woman, the semen and blood arise; that becomes the essence of the food-essence (*rasa*), and from that, this progeny is produced.

Just as fire, having encountered the wind, attains its full manifestation, so too the living soul (*jīva*), impelled by its own karma, enters the semen and, having properly united with the blood, becomes the progenitor of both bodies. Possessing the essential reality through the impurities derived from the woman and the man, it enters the womb and there, through the action of wind, fire, and water, it is moistened and thoroughly cooked; thus, through the growth of the semen and blood, beings are born as male, female, or neuter according to their common nature. Such is this form produced by the mother.

The embryo develops moment by moment, day by day, and month by month according to the prescribed rule; having become solidified, it consists of the mother's food-essence and its own self-sustaining essence. On the second day as well, it grows in this very manner every day, reaching the size of a thumb-joint like a water bubble. Then, some channels (nāḍīs) that were curved and facing downward become straight; on the left side there is Piṅgalā, and likewise on the right and the north. There are also Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Sapuṣpā, and Laṃbukā; these seven channels arise from the connection with the origin of the navel and serve as vehicles for transport.

That which is born first among those [channels] is sung as *sūṣumneti*; the illustrious *śaṅkhinī* and *cakruhū* are likewise born in sequence from the ten [directions]. From that *suṣumnā*, five joints (*parvan*) arise separately; from them, three hundred thousand [hair-pores] are born, and another fifty thousand are born from the head, pervading the body. O best of sages, there are three hundred and sixty bones in this body; in their respective parts, they serve as limbs and support the limbs of the bed [of the body]. In this body, the ten [channels] are to be known as the handfuls of water.
Just as seven *navas* (handfuls) of chyle are proclaimed [to be in the body], so too are seven of feces; eight *añjali*s of blood are declared, and six of phlegm are likewise mentioned.

Pitta is also five, and in this body there are four of urine. There are three of lymph (*annavasa*), two of marrow, and likewise one of fat. There is half an *añjali* of bone-marrow in the head, and the semen is exactly that much. By these subtle vital essences (*ojas*) the body is bound together; in this very manner it grows day by day, O ascetic. First the navel comes into being, then the head, the feet, and the hands—the affliction [of growth].
