O Sage, this body of his is vast, consisting of six limbs and other parts: the forehead, eyes, nose, ears, cheeks, the two jaws, the chin, the row of teeth, the tongue, the uvula, the head, hair, throat, shoulders, elbows, hands, nails, fingers, the two armpits, the thighs, the two sides, the back, the belly, the navel, the genitals, the buttocks, the anus, the thighs, the knees, the two shanks, the feet, the toes, and the body hair— all of which cover this body with skin both inside and out.

The vital airs (vāyus) cause movement from one place to another and also swiftly move the seven constituent elements (dhātus) within the body. These five winds in this body are proclaimed as being distinct: the wind called Prāṇa resides in the heart; the one called Apāna is situated in the anus; the one called Samāna is in the navel; Udāna is born in the region of the throat; and Vyāna stands pervading the entire body from head to foot. Furthermore, there are Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—these ten winds reside within the body among the seven constituents, while seven others reside in other locations.

Passing through the end of sweat and moisture, having thus reached the body at the time of birth, it emerges from the mother’s womb in great agony, crying out. In the ninth month, it falls to the earth like a sword.

Although its limbs are enveloped in pus, blood, feces, and urine, that living being, bewildered by an excess of suffering upon reaching the ground from the birth canal, runs outside while forgetting even itself. Tormented constantly by hunger and thirst, it surely desires only the breast. Growing day by day for a fortnight, a month, or a year...

In this world, one should become fully manifest through the subjects taught at the time of truth; he who always delights in what is truly dear to his parents and kinsmen, being constantly nurtured and flourishing year after year, will find that all of it, though perpetually his own, at that very moment must be completely abandoned as he moves toward the external. If he were to renounce everything and perceive the Self within the self, then by this alone he is liberated from the fears and sufferings of saṃsāra. (49) [Thus ends the twenty-second chapter of the Śrī Agasti Saṃhitā.]

[Chapter on Purification] (22) Agastya said: O Lord, you whose sole characteristic is non-dual bliss-consciousness and pure being, who shine forth as the inner and outer self with extremely sharp rays both within and without—here, the cause is indeed beginningless unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). O storehouse of penance, whether it be deficient or exceeding, in all cases it is perceived only externally through objects. Even that which is deficient, having reached the end of the objects within, becomes external to him. Therefore, know the Self within the Self itself without interruption, even while unmanifested by objects.

Whatever exists here in this phenomenal world, whether moving or unmoving, fashioned by the respective unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of each being, in all that consciousness dwells perpetually. This phenomenal world, as an effect, is indeed permeated everywhere by consciousness as its cause. Among beings here, it is through the elements that [consciousness appears]; this alone is consciousness here. Therefore, what else could there be other than this?
The Supreme Self, the individual self, Brahman, Truth—that is "Om"—and Knowledge, Bliss: all these are designations for consciousness. There is nothing higher than consciousness.

The inner reality is seen within all embodied beings, just as one sees pots and other objects within the earth; this is perceived by the awakened and the vigilant among all creatures. One might imagine something unseen here, yet love arises in this world for that which belongs to oneself and which is beneficial to one's own self. If it were not so, it would not be right that one perceives another as distinct; for living beings are diverse, and their effects are likewise of such a nature. How then, while purifying one's own conduct according to the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas, could one [behave otherwise]?

Sutīkṣṇa said: "Consciousness alone is established everywhere, even in its entirety; there is nothing else besides the Self. In this world, one does not know that reality which is being investigated by the gods. Through the loss of knowledge, one's austerity vanishes right there. One who desires to know all truths has perished through negligence. If one should behold the single supreme light, one sees it everywhere.

Desiring to see, one should behold that with an undistracted mind even amidst sense objects; one should behold that supreme consciousness and nothing else, even while sleeping. [Those who are] most wicked and cruel..."

Then, how do all those who are eternally excluded [from the truth] and seekers of various fruits perceive it? Tell me that. Due to negligence alone, one does not know what is held in one's own hand; such a person, though desiring to know, perceives only that which is utterly contemptible. O storehouse of penance, see for yourself with your whole being: everything everywhere is illuminated by Him who is Himself manifest as the very nature of Existence-Consciousness-Bliss. There is nothing else beyond Him—neither existent nor non-existent, nor anything distinct from those two. Even for the wise, they call that which veils Him "Ignorance" (avidyā), and it is this which arises within them.
Even while remaining within those very sense-objects, that sage perceives the unmanifested, hidden characteristics of pleasure, pain, and so forth belonging to all living beings;

he sees everything everywhere directly before him as consciousness pervading all objects. He who is pure and vigilant is never at any time enticed even by sense-objects; such a one directly beholds the Self. Even though he is of this nature, whoever thoroughly knows the Self—which is characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss, which is omnipresent—remains entirely undisturbed; he is thus truly alive even while living.

If one should think thus, "May it be so," then by the yoga of *pūraka* (inhalation), one should again bring the all-pervading consciousness from outside into oneself; having properly established that which resides everywhere within the foundation (*ādhāra*), one should meditate on Rāma with undistracted mind. Having diligently unified the air located within the body in ten ways at each respective place, one should perform the practice of *pūraka* with the breath in the form of a serpent’s mouth. Then, by means of consciousness, fire, and wind, one should ascend through the sequence of piercing the knots (*granthi-bheda*) and cross over the wind.

One should bring that wind of blissful consciousness, which has entered the mouth [of the central channel], into the range of that [channel's] opening. Impelled by it, one should lead it upward again and again toward the Supreme;

through the excellence of practice alone, one of undistracted mind pierces the lotus. Having reached the interior range of that [lotus] through that sequence, even if the *vīrāsana* posture is bound on the ground, there may be an interval within. If this very [wind] should pierce a second [lotus] as well, the wind situated within its end should lead the body upward, by means of the proper application of practice through the breaking of the knots of the heart.

There, at the joints where the connections are formed, that great [force] which has reached the beginning and the end, having thoroughly purified that body, ascends to the space between the eyebrows. There, in his two-petaled lotus, the extraordinary treasury of nectar flows forth as the nectar of immortality; by this alone is one prepared for immortality. One should again pierce that which resides in the sharp edge of the fifth joint. Thus, all knowledge becomes fruitful through that. Through dispassion (*vairāgya*) and renunciation (*tyāga*), one reaches that supreme state; indeed, O Lord of Yogis, there is no other path for him than renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). Having made both the external and internal [realities] one's own...

From the *mūlādhāra*, having ascended the path consisting of consciousness as far as the *dvādaśānta*, the yogi does not return again; O Indra among yogis, this path is not found in any other system, nor is it accepted by others, yet it is distinct and beautifully adorned by all. One should contemplate with a passion-free mind, directly realize Brahman, and become blissful. This alone is the goal of human endeavor here; there is nothing else whatsoever. One should never separate the Self from the yoga of unbroken bliss. "This is truth, this is truth"—even truth itself does not exist [as a separate entity]. Rāma is the supreme Brahman; there is nothing other than Rāma.

This *Agastyasaṃhitā*, which yields all desires, has been proclaimed by the high-souled Agastya, who is patient with the secrets of all scriptures; it is a lamp illuminating the world of the supreme self (*adhyātma*), a destroyer of ignorance, and a constant bestower of enjoyment and liberation, increasing longevity and health. Whether heard or seen, even when written, it purifies both externally and internally. Even a sinful soul shall be liberated and fit for union with Brahman (*brahmabhūya*) by one who beholds it even once from beginning to middle to end. One should contemplate it at all times.

One who recites this attains the entire world known as the yoga of Brahman-knowledge and shall obtain all desired security. In whose house a written manuscript of this remains, worshipped with honor, his longevity, health, and prosperity increase day by day; and through sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, his lineage flourishes. (50) [Thus ends the twenty-third chapter of the Śrī Agastya-saṃhitā. (23) Agastya said: This alone is the path to the City (the supreme abode), this action is higher than the highest; in Rāma alone resides the supreme light, which is Existence-Consciousness-Bliss.

The Supreme Light is the self of the manifest universe; having thoroughly examined the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas, Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Nārada, and others have determined that this sacrifice proceeds from Him. From those elements—both moving and non-moving—which are mutually intermingled, all beings were sacrificed. This All-Illuminating One, who has emerged from the *Tat*, is the Supreme embodied Self, distinct from the essential nature of the individual body. Though fivefold in nature, He becomes manifold through the differentiation of colors (castes), as expressed in such passages as "That which was [the syllable] 'Ya'... and so forth.

That which has no end whatsoever, because it is the nature of the cause, is the object of worship in the highest world; it is that in which everything is established. That which illuminates all else is the supreme light, inherently transcendent. Since it is the essence of perpetual exaltation, it always bestows prosperity. Therefore, one who desires liberation and worldly enjoyment should recite this with effort. Beyond this there is nothing higher; this is the *mantra* that expresses it. Of all *manus*, this alone is distinguished as supreme; this alone, having cast off the end, is the single letter "A."

When this mantra is worshipped, it generates this sacrifice. Beyond that, if these three are also [present]—along with Māyā, Manmatha, and the Vedas and so forth—rising together from the beginning, consisting of five syllables preceded by the *utkrama* (the upward progression)—from that sacrifice everything is born. The supreme mantra ending in *Candra* (the Moon) consists of four syllables ending in *Bhadra*. The wise know its fruit to be both of this world and the next. The six-syllable mantra, beginning and ending with each of the seeds Śrī, Māyā, and Manmatha, is for service; this mantra may also be four syllables.

Preceded by the seeds *Tāra* (Om), *Māyā* (Hrīṃ), and *Ramaṅga* (Klīṃ), this mantra has been declared in many ways as the bestower of all desired fruits. When joined with salutations to Candrabhadra and those respective seed-syllables, it is thus divided in many ways through the numbers six, seven, eight, nine, and so on. It is itself manifold through the sequence of one and so forth; yet this supreme "Svayaṃrāma" grants all desires even when not ending [in a specific way]. It is distinguished by its beginning with the feet or beginning with the word, and it is further distinguished by its specific variations. Its worship is differentiated according to the infinite distinctions of the qualified practitioners of the mantras.

Brahmā, Agastya, Śiva, and I myself have declared that these [syllables] are indeed the Gāyatrī; she is called the deity of the Ṛc, Yajus, and Sāman. She is the seed and power (bīja-śakti) of both the prior and the posterior, having enjoyment and liberation as her purpose. With the seed-syllables joined at the beginning and end, one performs the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) along with the Praṇavas. [One should assign them] to the left and right, to the left and right eyebrows, to the eyes, the ears, the cheeks, the jaws, the lips, the roots of the teeth, the tongue and its root, the throat and the hump (kakuda), the breasts, the shoulders, the arms, the hands, the sides, the back, the heart, and the navel.

One should place [the syllables] on the back, the navel, the two sides of the chest, the thighs, the knees, the shanks, and the feet, manifesting the forms of Sītā and Rāma by means of the seed-syllable of Śakti. One should perform the *saṃhṛti-nyāsa* (dissolution placement) starting from the feet up to the head; likewise, one should perform the *utpatti-nyāsa* (origination placement) here, starting from the navel and proceeding upwards. Next, one should perform the *pratyakṣara-nyāsa* (syllable-by-syllable placement), followed by the *mūrti-nyāsa* (form placement). Then one should perform the *tattva-nyāsa* (elemental placement) and also the *keśava-ādi-nyāsa* (placement beginning with Keśava). Furthermore, one should perform the *sarvāṅga-nyāsa* (whole-body placement) using the entire mantra. One should meditate upon the supreme light within the lotus of the heart.

Having worshipped that God, who is higher than the highest, with various offerings right there, one should recite [the mantra] in some secluded place while meditating on Rāma with undistracted mind: [One should meditate on Him] resembling a dense cloud, clothed in garments the color of lightning, and Sītā, who shines like refined gold, seated upon His lap; their hearts, arms, and eyes joined together as they gaze at each other with devotion; Him touching her chin with the tip of His right hand, which has curly locks of hair, and her breast with His other hand; Him delighting her with repeated jests, while she is solely intent on chewing betel-leaf; [and Him who is] all...

The pair of Śrī Rāma and Sītā is like a couple of man and woman resplendent with beauty, bestowing the fruit of all prosperity and liberation. One should constantly perform acts such as recitation, fire-offerings, and worship;

whatever [is done] shall become infinite—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. This mantra, which expresses this very thing, is the accomplisher of every purpose; this supreme mantra, expressing the existent as the existent, is victorious. By the mere chanting or even the remembrance of the one whose self is Rāma, one does not accumulate sin even after killing a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra.

Whatever sin has been accumulated, such as the killing of village animals or wild beasts, this mantra of Rāma—consisting of two syllables and having Rāma as its soul—destroys it all without remainder. Worshipped by those who have arisen from the corners of the mouth and other parts [of the body], it wipes away and swiftly destroys even the sin incurred by drinking liquor. Through the auspicious recitation of this mantra of Rāma, every sin arising from false knowledge or the eating of forbidden food dissolves. Furthermore, whatever sin has been acquired through stealing the gold of a Vedic scholar, or the theft of gems and other valuables, is likewise destroyed.
Even that [sin] he would thus destroy; having gone to his own mother out of delusion, Rāma would destroy even that by means of the *upasthāna* mantra.

Whatever has been accumulated through association with the most wicked of great sinners (*mahāpātakin*), he would destroy that through conversation, sharing a bed, sitting together, and eating together. Whatever sin has arisen from the intentional killing of father or mother, he destroys it entirely, including that which arises in the three periods of time. Whether it be the sin of those who kill a brother, a friend, or a sister, or of a betrayer of trust, or even of a child...

Even poison, weapons, murderers, or the wives and children of one’s preceptor—whatever has arisen from the wicked—dissolves entirely by the mere contemplation of this [Mantra]. Furthermore, when practiced according to the path taught by a true Guru, this very Mantra, whose essence is Rāma, destroys heaps of sin; even that sin which is not removed by penances and other rites at holy sites such as Prayāga, it shall quickly destroy. What need is there for various gifts of gold equal to one's own weight? Even a tiny fragment...

Even that sin which has been committed will be destroyed; even that accumulated sin, that great-rooted transgression, perishes entirely by the mere remembrance of that mantra. [Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the Śrī Agastisaṃhitā. (24) Sutīkṣṇa said: O knower of reality, O you who are devoted to Brahman, O treasure of asceticism, O soul of Rāma, the supreme, imperishable reality of Brahman has been perfectly demonstrated by you in its entirety and in many ways. However, the ritual procedure for the six-syllabled mantra...

"O Lord, O Great Sage, you have explained the knowledge of other Rāma-mantras and their practice; but is there another procedure for the six-syllabled mantra? Tell me everything, O observer of noble vows, for I am devoted to you. Agastya said: "O Sutīkṣṇa, listen; I shall speak again to you who are faithful. Because of your effort and devotion, you are indeed the best of Vaiṣṇavas. Those who hear the story of Viṣṇu, speak of the deeds of Hari, sing of Hari with unrestrained throats, and dance beautifully with voices sweet as they are filled with tears of joy—"

With their limbs covered in horripilation and overflowing with bliss, they stumble at every step; they cry out loudly, "Śrī Rāma! Rāma! and laugh. Endowed with such qualities, those Vaiṣṇavas who are absorbed in the Self-realized state shall indeed grant liberation to all in due course. Listen, O best of Brahmins: the mantras of Rāma grant swift liberation even without initiation and without the performance of *puraścaraṇa*; by the mere recitation performed according to the Vaiṣṇava ritual of *nyāsa*, they bestow perfection upon everyone in general.

O highly fortunate one, the specific details regarding the performance of the rites for the Manus and for Rāghava will indeed be explained here and there in great detail according to the rules. However, they know the six-syllabled rite (*ṣaḍakṣara-vidhāna*) to be the archetype for all. O Sage, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) must be performed first for everyone; all the previously mentioned ritual placements (*nyāsa*) should be carried out with effort, O observer of good vows.

Among all these rites, embodied beings have the right to participate. All those situated in the stages of life (*āśrama*) are eligible for the mantras. It should always be practiced by those seeking liberation and those who are dispassionate.

The best of the Raghus is to be worshipped by those ascetics whose minds are disciplined, just as the Praṇava is; and the previously mentioned procedure for initiation (dīkṣā) should be performed by the most excellent preceptors. Having been initiated, one should perform the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) according to the respective mantras. O best of beings, breath control (prāṇāyāma) for all should be done with the Gāyatrī. One should perform the consecration of water with the root mantra (mūla-mantra), as well as the sprinkling (mārjana), the drinking of water, the casting of the offering-water (argha), and the purification (mārjana). One should perform the worship of Sītā with her specific mantra and likewise the recitation (japa) of the root mantra. The rites of standing in attendance (upasthāna) and so forth should be performed right there by the best of the twice-born.

I bow to the lotus-eyed one situated in the center of the solar orb, accompanied by Sītā and Rāma; salutations to the supreme teacher of Māñjaneja (Hanumān). Salutations to Vāmadeva, to the Lord of lights, to the witness of all worlds, and to Him whose form is supreme bliss. Salutations to the divine Raghunātha, the Great Compassionate One, who bestows joy upon Kauśika (Viśvāmitra) and possesses the universal form.

He who performs this [rite] at the three junctions of time shall himself become Rāma. Thus, the preliminary practice (*puraścaryā*) for all is prescribed according to the stated path; having thus mastered the mantra, the practitioner [should perform it] every day.

O Sage, one who is firm in his vows [should meditate on] the all-pervading Lord, who has four arms and bears the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; who wears a crown, possesses noble limbs, and is adorned with a forest garland; whose left side is graced by Sītā; who wears yellow garments; who resembles pure crystal and blazes with splendor. Or else, one may meditate on the two-armed God, whose luster is like a blue lotus, who resembles many suns, and who is seated upon a lotus; accompanied by the Goddess on his left side, who has the radiance of gold, and attended by the wise Lakṣmaṇa of golden hue holding a parasol.

Having diligently worshipped with mental offerings many times by numerous divine attendants, and having meditated for a long time upon that which has arisen from the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), one who has restrained his senses should perform the recitation of the root mantra with discipline. Thereafter, one should perform external worship with materials acquired through righteous means; O best of sages, worship performed with wealth acquired through unjust means is fruitless. O sharpest of sages, I shall now describe external worship again: in one's own home, on a pure patch of ground smeared with cow-dung and provided with a canopy...

To the Great-souled Sage, who was seated upon a pure seat in a place adorned on all sides with perfumes, flowers, and the like, and beautifully decorated everywhere with songs and instrumental music, he performed worship in many ways with various services— using sandalwood, agallochum, musk, camphor, flowers, and the like, well-ground with snow— and with blossoming *karavīra* flowers,
white and red fragrant blooms, *punnāga*, *puṣpaka*, and buds, as well as *śatapatraka*, jasmine, *mallikā*, *kahlāra*, lotuses, *pāṭala*, and *ketakī* flowers.

One should worship the Joy of the Raghus (Rāma) among all Vaiṣṇavas; the best of practitioners, knowing the ritual rules, should diligently perform the worship of the conch three times a day according to the injunctions. Indeed, for a Vaiṣṇava who worships Hari even without the worship of the conch, it is certain that although he has worshipped Him perfectly, He remains as if unworshipped. [He should offer] many fragrant incenses produced from guggulu, along with numerous wicks soaked in oil and arranged in various ways, and many lamps carefully placed upon lotuses and svastikas.
Furthermore, one should cause [the offering] to be carried around in the form of a crane or a swan day after day in front of Raghunātha.

Having offered with great effort that which has been prepared, pure, radiant, and pleasing—consisting of food, snacks, and edibles placed before him, including soups, cakes, ghee, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and excellent sugar; adorned with many side-dishes, beautiful, accompanied by ghee, and beloved for its curd; and having given to Raghunātha betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*) made charming with areca nut (*pūgīphala*) and pieces of camphor—one shall attain all desires.

O Sage, the procedure previously described has been stated here in brief for all Rāma-mantras; performed in this very manner, whether at the three times of day or at a single time, one should always worship in this way. Having become a sovereign lord of the entire earth, one shall indeed become Rāma himself in this world. [Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter of the Śrī Agastisaṃhitā. Agastya said: O Sutīkṣṇa, I shall now declare to you the secret, the essence of all practices, the most excellent of all that has been spoken.

O best of sages, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, during the Puṣya nakṣatra under the Punarvasu asterism, when Jupiter was in its exaltation and the five planets were in their positions of strength, and when the sun had entered Aries and the ascendant known as Cancer had arrived, the Supreme Person appeared in the womb of Kauśalyā. On that day, one should always observe a fast and a vow; there, being devoted to the Lord of the Raghus, one should perform a vigil on earth. Then, on the morning of the tenth day, having performed the twilight rituals and the daily rites, one should worship [the deity] according to the rules.

With devotion and according to one’s means, one should feed Brāhmaṇas with devotion and satisfy them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), as well as with cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and the like, and with garments and ornaments.

One should worship the devotees of Rāma with great effort and supreme joy. He who performs the Śrī Rāmanavamī vow in this manner with devotion, having reduced to ashes even many sins accumulated over numerous births, goes indeed to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. This dharma is the sole means for the attainment of both worldly enjoyment and liberation for all; whether impure or otherwise...

Having prepared this excellent fast with flour-cakes, one shall become worthy of worship by all beings, just like Rāma himself. That lowest of men who eats on the ninth day of Rāma’s festival is the most base of humans;

he is cooked in the terrible Kumbhīpāka hells. He consumes the sins of the three worlds, and his merit becomes fruitless. That lowest of men who disregards Rāma’s ninth-day festival out of atheism shall not attain the highest state until the moon and stars perish. Without performing the Rāmanavamī vow—the best of all vows—do not perform any other vows.

Therefore, one shall become a partaker of their fruit; even many well-known secret sins, however great they may be, perish through the Śrī Rāmanavamī vow. O Sage, by fasting for even a single Śrī Rāmanavamī, a man becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done and is liberated from all sins. O best of sages, a man who offers an image of Śrī Rāma on the Rāmanavamī day according to the prescribed rite is liberated; of this there is no doubt. Sutīkṣṇa said: [Tell me] the procedure for the offering of the image of Śrī Rāma.

"How, O Sage, will you tell me in detail about my devotee Rāma? Agastya said: "O learned one, I shall describe that supreme gift of the image, as well as its ritual procedure with care, since you are indeed the best among Vaiṣṇavas. On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, having subdued the senses, one should perform the morning bath according to the rules, preceded by the cleansing of the teeth, whether in a river, a pond, a well, a lake, or a spring. Then, while remembering Rāghava in the heart, one should perform the twilight prayers and other rites."

Having returned home, O best of Brahmins, one should invite a self-controlled householder Brahmin who is devoted to the Vedas and Shastras, intent on the worship of Śrī Rāma, of virtuous conduct, free from anger, knowledgeable in the ritual procedures, and whose sole means of practice is the Rāma-mantra; having honored him with devotion, one should choose him while praying thus: "O most excellent of the twice-born, I shall perform the gift of an image of Śrī Rāma; please be my preceptor (ācārya) therein. Having said, "I am pleased; you are indeed Śrī Rāma himself," one should then bathe that Brahmin with clarified butter (ājya).

Having worshipped with oil and bathed while meditating on Rāghava in his heart, wearing white garments and bearing cool-smelling garlands, adorned and consecrated, and having performed his midday rites, he should devoutly feed the preceptor at great length with pure (sāttvika) foods. He himself should likewise eat, remembering Rāma in his heart. Having eaten but one meal, the preceptor—firm in his vow and free from fear—should listen to the divine narrative of the Name and spend the remainder of the day, O Sage. In the evening, he should perform the twilight prayers and other rites, keeping Rāma in mind.

Remembering this, the preceptor, having conquered his senses and with his mind offered to Śrī Rāma, should sleep there himself in a secluded place along with the disciple. Then, rising up pleased, he should bathe and quickly complete all the morning rites according to the prescribed rules. Thereafter, O sinless one, becoming composed in mind and accompanied by learned men, he should, in the northern part of his own house, construct an excellent pavilion for the gift-offering—having four doors, adorned with banners and the like, provided with a canopy and beautiful archways, delightful, very lofty, and strewn with flowers.

Adorned with conches, discs, and Hanumān at the eastern gate; adorned with Garuḍa, the Śārṅga bow, and arrows at the southern [gate]; adorned with the mace and the khaṭvāṅga staff at the western [gate];

and adorned with lotuses, svastikas, and blue [emeralds] at the northern [gate]; with its fourfold courtyard and so forth, its hand-sized altar-ledge extended in length, well-restrained by instrumental music, singing, and other [performances], one should there, with a joyful mind, have the learned recite the "Auspicious Day" (Puṇyāha). Then, O Rāma, one should make this formal resolve (saṃkalpa):

O Sage, on this Rāmanavamī, one intent on the worship of Rāma, having approached the eight southern directions and worshipped according to the prescribed rites, shall offer this gold-made image of Rāma, well-adorned, for the pleasure of Śrī Rāma, to a wise devotee of Rāma. May Rāma, being pleased, quickly remove my many great sins— those accumulated and practiced over many births— even as he holds the gold-made image of Rāma, fashioned from a *pala* of weight, in his two arms.

O great sage, [one should meditate on her] holding Jānakī upon her left lap, while with her right hand she displays the *jñānamudrā*. Embracing the goddess with her lower left hand, she sits resplendent upon a throne fashioned from two *palas* of silver. Then, having performed the ritual bath with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and worshipped according to the rules, one should remain diligent and self-controlled, performing the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) preceded by the root mantra. Having thus performed the rites during the day, one should then keep a vigil at night; accompanied by devotees of Rāma, one should listen to the divine story of Rāma and engage in dance and song.

The wise man, having worshipped Rāma in various ways with divine hymns according to the rules and with devotion throughout the day and night, should then rise at dawn. Having completed the rites of bathing, the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), and so forth according to the rules, he should worship Rāma with a well-concentrated mind. Then, the knower of mantras, being composed, should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) in the previously mentioned lotus-shaped pit (*kuṇḍa*) or on the sacrificial mound (*asthaṇḍila*) using the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*). Following the prescribed ritual, he should offer one hundred and eight oblations of milk-rice mixed with clarified butter into the common fire (*laukikāgni*), while remembering the Name of the Lord with single-minded focus.

O Sage, having fully satisfied the preceptor with devotion, one should worship him with two jeweled earrings, various finger-rings, perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and many kinds of beautiful, most charming garments. Then, remembering Rāma, one should give [the gift] while reciting this mantra: "I, who am Rāma, offer this gold image of Rāma, well-adorned and covered with a pair of yellow cloths, to the wise devotee of Rāma, for the sake of Śrī Rāma’s pleasure. May Rāma, being pleased, quickly destroy even my many great sins. Others [should do likewise].

He should give cows, gold, and so forth to them according to what is right and according to his capacity; or, being composed, he should give a pair of garments and grain according to his wealth. He should eat together with the Brāhmaṇas and give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). He is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa; there is no doubt in this matter. O observer of good vows, he obtains the fruit of the Tulāpuruṣa gift. He is certainly liberated from the sins accumulated over many births. What is the use of saying more here? Liberation stands within his very hand. [This occurs] at the highly meritorious Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse in its entirety.

"O observer of noble vows, whatever fruit is obtained by mortals through the performance of gifts such as the *tulāpuruṣa* and others, that same fruit is obtained by them through this gift. [Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the glorious *Agastisaṃhitā*. Sutīkṣṇa said: "O Sage, for the most part all men are poor and wretched; they are indeed incapable of this gift. Tell me, O Lord, what should be done for them? Agastya said: "O highly fortunate one, those who are unable [to give much] should give according to their own means—even half a *pala*, or half of that, or half of that again."

Furthermore, O Sage, one should perform this vow even without stinginess regarding wealth; for there is no place where one fears to behold most terrible torments. Even if one possesses nothing, having fasted on the ninth day according to the rules and performed a vigil with devotion accompanied by the devotees of Rāma, one should worship according to the injunctions while remembering Rāma with a devoted mind, O Sage.

Reciting the *Māyā-Ramā-Ananga* (Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kāma) mantra, or the single-syllable (*ekākṣara*) mantra, according to the rules, one whose excellence is established through all the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) should bathe in the morning according to the rules and—

One should perform the rites beginning with the twilight prayers (sandhyā) and, endowed with faith, give cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and other gifts according to one's wealth to learned devotees of Śrī Rāmacandra.

Then, with devotion, one should break the fast (pāraṇa) together with the brāhmaṇas. He who performs this with devotion is liberated from all sins. When the day of Śrī Rāmanavamī arrives, the mortal of deluded intellect who does not observe the fast sinks into the Kumbhīpāka hell. Furthermore, he who does not give anything whatsoever for the sake of Rāma according to his ability [also suffers]. Sutīkṣṇa said:

"O Great Sage, you have stated that worship should be performed during the eight watches (*yāmāṣṭaka*) with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*); tell me, O observer of noble vows, how is that so? Agastya said: The six-syllabled mantra (*ṣaḍakṣara*), the king of mantras, is the *tāraka-brahman* for all [mantras]; therefore, worship by means of it is highly praised. Worship should be diligently performed according to the procedure of the tenth chapter, as well as for the deities of the door, the pedestal (*pīṭha*), the limbs (*aṅga*), and the enclosures (*āvṛti*). Here, the 'sealing' (*sannirodhana*) is indeed the 'veiling' (*avaguṇṭhana*) performed properly with their respective mudrās; thus it should be done while praying with devotion."

Then, O Sage, one should perform the worship of the conch according to the previously mentioned procedure. With devotion, one should respectfully sprinkle the water-pot situated on the left side, the articles for worship, and the vessel; one should also recite the mantra over oneself. One should perform the worship of the conch every watch (prati-yāma), thus remembering the mantra. In this same manner, one should diligently prepare the vessels and implements in the southern direction. The wise practitioner should offer nine new cloths to the Lord and satisfy Him with libations. He should also give golden sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*) to the Lord according to his capacity, as well as various jewels of diverse kinds.

One should diligently offer incense containing camphor, rubbed with *himāmbu* (snow-water), along with fragrant substances, red dyes, and saffron. One should perform all the ritual services (*upacāra*) with the root mantra and worship [the deity] with *kalhāra*, *ketakī*, *jātī*, *puṇnāga*, and other flowers—such as *campaka*, *śatapatra*, and other sweet-smelling, most enchanting blossoms.

Ringing the bell, one should present incense and a lamp to Him, and with devotion, according to the prescribed rite, offer edible foods, snacks, and so forth to the God. Thus [one worships] the God together with His appurtenances.

O Sage, one is liberated from terrible sins committed over ten million births—sins that are manifold and most cruel—and at that very moment, one becomes like Lord Rāma himself. This Śrī Rāmanavamī vow, which is pure and destructive of sin, has been proclaimed for the benefit of all the world. O Sage, whether fashioned from metal, stone, or even wood, in whatever manner and to whomever it may be given, by bestowing it upon a Brāhmaṇa according to one's capacity on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, along with great gifts and the like...

It should be equal [to the standard rite] when performed with Rāma as the objective; one should perform everything with great devotion, without any stinginess regarding wealth. Seated in solitude, one should recite [the mantra] until the tenth day; by that alone, the *puraścaraṇa* is accomplished.

On the tenth day, one should feed the twice-born with various kinds of foods, both solid and soft, and give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability. By this, one becomes successful in one’s purpose, and Rāma immediately becomes pleased. Remaining silent, one descends [from the state of rebirth], free from the cycle of returning to the womb. Even that sin which is not removed by twelve hundred or eight hundred [recitations] is destroyed.

All that goes to dissolution on the day of Śrī Rāmanavamī. However, for one who does not know the recitation of the Rāma-mantras, he should fast and remember Rāma with single-minded devotion, preceded by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). But for one who has received the mantra from a guru, he should perform worship according to the rules at every watch of the night, preceded by *nyāsa*, with a concentrated mind. Even those seeking liberation always observe the vow of Śrī Rāmanavamī; he is liberated from all sins and attains the eternal Brahman. (34) [Thus ends the section in the Śrī Agasti-saṃhitā]
Chapter Twenty-Seven. Agastya said: On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, Rāma himself, who is Hari, was born under the asterism of Punarvasu.

Even if it is seen for only a very short duration on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, that auspicious Śrī Rāmanavamī bestows all desires; it is said to be superior to ten million suns.

If the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra is joined with the asterism of Punarvasu, whatever rite whatsoever is performed with devotion on that highly meritorious day dedicated to Rāma, that [act becomes inexhaustible].

Therefore, one should especially perform fasting and keeping vigil on the auspicious Rāma-navamī. Whatever little one may give according to one’s means on the Rāma-navamī, all of that becomes equal to a great gift (mahādāna). If a person performs the Rāma-vrata on the Rāma-navamī, that human being obtains the fruit of the Tulā-puruṣa gift and other such offerings. One obtains that same fruit by performing the Śrī Rāma-navamī vrata as is gained by repeatedly performing great gifts at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse. Therefore, one should vigilantly observe the fast on the Rāma-navamī. Mā... [text ends]

One does not obtain a good womb, nor would one become Rāma himself, if the ninth [tithi] is overlapped by the eighth; therefore, those devoted to Viṣṇu must avoid such an overlap. Fasting should be observed on the ninth day, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should indeed take place on the tenth.

[One should meditate upon] the all-pervading Lord, dark as the petal of a blue lotus, wearing yellow garments, two-armed, with beautiful eyes, seated upon a divine lion-throne. He is surrounded by Vasiṣṭha and others, wears a jeweled crown, is skillful in conversation with Sītā, and is adorned with divine fragrances and the like. With two bows in his hands, he is served nearby by Lakṣmaṇa, and likewise by Bharata and Śatrughna at his sides.

Meditating upon Him who is served by them with a single-minded heart, one should daily mutter the twelve-syllable mantra. Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and the mantra-sandhyā every day, one should always worship Śrī Rāma at the three junctions of the day.

Sutīkṣṇa said: O Blessed One, best among yogis, proficient in all scriptures! What is the ultimate reality? What is the supreme object of recitation? What is the knowledge that is the means to liberation? O best of sages, I wish to know all of this; please tell it to me. Agastya said: O Sutīkṣṇa, you are highly fortunate; listen, for I shall speak according to the truth—that which...

That stainless light which transcends the Raṃ Yamunā is the fruit; that alone is the supreme reality, the cause of the state of Kaivalya. "Śrī Rāma" is the supreme mantra to be recited, known as the *Tāraka* and designated as Brahman. Those who know the Vedas understand it to be the destroyer of sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. For those who always utter "Śrī Rāma, Rāma, Rāma," there will be both worldly enjoyment and liberation;

of this there is no doubt. Having offered salutations, I shall proclaim the faultless Rāma-Kṛṣṇa. One should meditate upon Him at the foot of the Kalpa-tree, situated in the center of a beautiful jeweled circle within the city of Ayodhyā.

In the center of that [mandala], one should have a beautiful jeweled lion-throne made, upon which is an eight-petaled lotus encrusted with various gems; this may be fashioned of gold or silver for the sake of the Joy of the Raghus (Rāma). At his sides, Bharata and Śatrughna should be depicted as bearers of the royal umbrella and fly-whisks.

A wise man should have Lakṣmaṇa fashioned holding two bows. He should be dark-complexioned like a sapphire, seated on his father’s lap, with tender limbs and large eyes, clothed in garments the color of lightning, and resplendent with a crown shining like ten million suns, adorned with jeweled necklaces, armlets, and gem-studded earrings.

One should draw a six-cornered [diagram] adorned with golden or silver jeweled bracelets, anklets, and a waist-cord; its chest graced by the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, and beautified by a pearl necklace. In the absence [of such materials], one should place the Joy of the Raghus upon a pedestal of bilva wood, endowed with two garments and decorated with divine jewels. One should worship the Lord of Gods, accompanied by the eight Śaktis, in due order. First uttering the Praṇava (Oṃ), one should then say the word "Namaḥ," and after pronouncing the word "Bhagavat," [one should say] "Vāsudevāya."

Then, with the mantra "Obeisance to the Self of all beings, the Self of the Yoga-pīṭha," one should offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) into the center of that [pīṭha]. Once the pīṭha has been thus worshipped, one should invoke the Deity and worship Him. Having performed the ritual services (upacāras) beginning with the water offering (arghya) and ending with incense and the lamp, one should then request permission from the Lord of Devas and worship His retinue. All [the rites], beginning with the Heart-mantra and following the sequence of the six, should be performed within the six-cornered compartments using the root mantra; likewise, the sixteen services are to be performed. One should also worship Indra and the other world-protectors (lokapālas), as well as Vasiṣṭha and the other sages, using the mantras of all the guardians of the directions.

One should worship [him] endowed with devotion; one should cause the Arghya, joined with Aśoka flowers, to be offered to the God, saying: "For the sake of slaying the Ten-faced one, for the establishment of Dharma, for the destruction of the Dānavas, and for the death of the Daityas, Hari himself was born as Rāma for the protection of the virtuous. O sinless one, accept this Arghya given by me along with my brothers.

One should especially worship the Joy of the Raghus at every watch (pratiyāma) with Purāṇas, hymns, Vedic recitations (pārāyaṇa), and by means of beautiful dances, songs, and instrumental music, thus passing the remainder of the night.

Having bathed at dawn, having muttered the Gāyatrī, and having performed the Sandhyā prayers, one should mentally meditate upon the Lord of Gods with the ten-syllable mantra. Various types of Nyāsa have been described by you;
then, having prostrated before the God of Gods, one should worship Him within the heart as before. [Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter of the Śrī Agasti Saṃhitā. Sutīkṣṇa said:

O wise one, best among those who know the Śrutis and Smṛtis, you have previously described many kinds of Nyāsa along with the application of mantras. How, then, should one who is incapable of that perform it?

"Tell me, O Great Sage. Agastya said: "Nyāsa is the armor of mantra; one devoid of nyāsa does not grant success. Therefore, those desiring accomplishment should perform nyāsas with great effort, especially for all mantras that are non-Vaiṣṇava. First is the nyāsa beginning with Keśava and Kīrti; after that is the Tattva-nyāsa. Then there is the nyāsa known as Paramahaṃsa, which is called Praṇava-nyāsa. One should likewise employ the Mātṛkā joined with the Bindu, the pure [Mātṛkā] joined with the Manmatha (Kāma-bīja), joined with Māyā and the Vedādi, and likewise beginning with the Praṇava."

Having established the internal *mātṛkā-cakra*, one should perform the practice (*anuṣṭhāna*). O best of sages, the entire practice of this must be performed. If one is incapable, then by reciting the mantra alone while remaining self-restrained day after day, one attains all desires; with Rāma, one shall attain Rāma. Sutīkṣṇa said: O Brahmin, I have heard from you the procedure for the worship and other rites of Rāma of wondrous deeds, along with its secrets, in many ways; and especially the procedure for the ten-syllable and other mantras, which is the singular means for attaining Brahman, when properly performed according to rule a hundred times.

"Now I wish to hear clearly the procedure for installation (*pratiṣṭhā*): when, where, and how? Since you are omniscient, tell me, O Master; for I have faith in you, and you are compassionate. Agastya said: "O Brahmin, you have asked well regarding that which is the most secret of secrets. He who beholds this supreme and meritorious [image] installed according to the prescribed rite becomes the most meritorious in the world and is instantly liberated from sin. Even the Grandfather (Brahmā) would not be able to describe the fruit of Śrī Rāma’s installation, nor even Maheśa, even in a thousand [lives]."

O Sage, by whatever means, in whatever manner, or wherever it may be, if this has been performed by anyone in this world, you are most blessed. One should not wait for a specific time, nor especially for an auspicious ritual (vidhi). As soon as devotion has arisen, then the descendant of Raghu should be installed. Alternatively, on the ninth day, or on a bright day in the month of Māgha, when the moon and stars are favorable, the best of the Raghus should be installed. Or, with a concentrated mind, in the full month of Mārgaśīrṣa or Vaiśākha, one should perform the installation of Rāghava, free from the defects of ignorance and other such faults.

One should perform [the installation] according to the rules, with devotion, according to one's capacity, and with great effort. For the installation of Śrī Gopāla, the month of Śrāvaṇa is always recommended; for Narasiṃha, Vaiśākha is recommended; and for Keśava, Caitra is also recommended. For Rāmacandra, Māgha is recommended when it is joined with the Bala constellation (Mṛgaśīrṣa); for Ananta as well, Māgha is suitable; but for others, it may be done according to one's preference. However, the best of the Raghus (Rāma) may be installed at all times and in all places. There is no requirement for an auspicious moment (*lagna*), nor for the lunar day (*tithi*), the day of the week (*vāra*), or the strength of the asterism (*nakṣatra*). On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, Rāma should be installed by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).

A fortunate man who performs the installation of Śrī Rāmacandra during the month of Māgha, when it is endowed with auspicious power, obtains all his desires. Likewise, by performing it according to the rules in the months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Vaiśākha, or during a highly meritorious solar eclipse at Kurukṣetra according to the prescribed rites, a mortal shall obtain that same merit which is acquired through the Tulāpuruṣa and other great gifts. That man who performs the installation of Rāmacandra according to the injunctions, having enjoyed all worldly pleasures, [attains] Nārāyaṇa...

The family shall not only flourish further for more than hundreds of millions of kalpas, but no one in that lineage shall ever be unlearned, nor foolish, nor poor, nor even a non-Vaiṣṇava, at any time or in any place. On an auspicious day, one should have a beautiful image of Śrī Rāma fashioned according to the rules, whether out of metal or wood; and likewise images of Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā, and especially Hanumān. Sītā should be made resembling gold, and Lakṣmaṇa should be the same.

Having purified the temple of the deity, one should diligently clean the excellent site for construction, avoiding wood, clay, and similar materials; one should dig that auspicious spot so that the growth of *tulasī* may occur there. Then, as before, the wise one should fill it with stones, sand, and other materials, and construct a paved floor for the excellent dwelling place.
Avoiding wood, clay, and the like, and using many pure, beautiful, and extensive stone slabs, one should, as before, raise the ground level in the area of the divine residence by two cubits.

One should cause a wide and charming enclosure wall to be built, provided there with four gate-towers (*gopura*). One should construct a beautiful pedestal (*pīṭha*) made of stone, excellent, elevated, two cubits in length, and perfectly square. O Sage, one should depict Hanumān on the front part of the pedestal. One should perform the purification of the pedestal according to the procedure to be described hereafter. Furthermore, one should draw Sugrīva in the southeast quarter; Bharata in the south; Vibhīṣaṇa in the southwest; Lakṣmaṇa in the west; and Aṅgada in the northwest. Śa... [text ends]

One should draw Trughna in the north and Ṛkṣanāyaka in the northeast; then, one should depict Śrī Rāmacandra upon the pedestal according to the prescribed rite, whether made of gold, silver, or copper.

Or, O Sage, one may fashion a very beautiful square diagram on stone, measuring either thirty-two fingers or sixteen fingers, and place that yantra at the site for the installation of the deity. First, one should perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) for seven, five, or three days, following the rules when the moon and stars are auspicious, and one should offer prayers to Gaṇeśa.

For the pacification of all obstacles, one should worship a golden image accompanied by two garments and offer it to a poor Brāhmaṇa who has a large family. O Sage, one should have it performed according to the rules through any method whatsoever—whether by the path of meditation on the single-syllable mantra, or by the ten-syllable rite, or by the Anuṣṭubh verse, or by the twelve-syllable path—of the image of Śrī Rāma. [Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter of the Śrī Agasti Saṃhitā. Sutīkṣṇa:

"O best of sages, tell me, how is the path of the ten-syllable mantra and others? O most excellent one, explain this to me along with its secret meaning, for I am devoted to you. Agastya said: "Excellent! I shall speak the truth to you; listen attentively to me. [One should meditate on] Rāghava, who is adorned by Sītā upon his left lap, two-armed, and large-eyed; who touches the circle of Sītā’s breasts with his left hand; who holds the *jñānamudrā* (the gesture of knowledge) rather than any other; who is beautiful to the world; who is further graced by the bow-wielding Lakṣmaṇa; and who resembles ten million gods of love (*Kandarpa*) in compassion."

One should visualize the Lord seated in the center of a lotus in the beautiful *vīrāsana* posture, attended by Hanumān before him—thus making the scene enchanting. This ten-syllable mantra has been declared according to the rules by the best of sages.

The All-pervading Lord is dark as the petal of a blue lotus, wearing yellow garments, two-armed, with eyes like lotuses, and seated upon a divine lion-throne. He is surrounded by Vasiṣṭha and others, adorned with necklaces and jeweled crowns, skillful in conversation with Sītā, and beautified by divine perfumes and the like. He is served from nearby by Lakṣmaṇa, who holds two bows in his hands, and also by Śatrughna and Bharata.

One who has been initiated should daily meditate upon Śrī Rāma, who is adorned on both sides and is not restless; one should constantly recite the twelve-syllable mantra preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa). Having performed the ritual of the mantra-sandhyā, one should always worship Him at the three junctions of the day—the all-pervading Lord who sports with Sītā, who resembles a dark cloud, who delights in Vṛṣākapīndra, and who was remembered by Vasiṣṭha. One should meditate on Him as He stands behind Lakṣmaṇa, who is beautifully adorned and holds two bows, while the son of Sumitrā stands before Him holding His bow and arrows. One should meditate on the all-pervading Lord, who is clad in yellow garments and is ever intent on the welfare of all the worlds.

O Sage, by chanting the seven-syllabled mantra, one is liberated from all sins. Meditating on Him who resembles a water-laden cloud and holds a bow and arrow in His hands, and chanting the eight-syllabled mantra, one then becomes Rama himself. Furthermore, meditating on Him who possesses arms adorned with the *jñānamudrā*, who is served by Hanumān, and who is surrounded by Śatrughna, Bharata, and Lakṣmaṇa, and chanting the single-syllabled mantra, one becomes a vessel for enjoyment. O best of sages, there are indeed many other forms; one should diligently install any one of these forms after reciting the Vaiṣṇava mantras and the root mantra.

Then, the wise preceptor should properly perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) and the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) for the mantra of the God Hanumān according to the prescribed rules;
thereafter, he should diligently perform them for the mantras of Lakṣmaṇa, the son of the Wind-god, as well as for Śatrughna, Bharata, and the others. Sutīkṣṇa said:

"O Sage, O ocean of compassion, you ought to tell me, your devotee, the entire procedure for the mantras of Lakṣmaṇa and the others. Agastya said: "Listen, I shall explain everything to you in great detail and in many ways."

Having extracted the letter preceded by *ra* (Ra) and joined with the mark of the bindu (Ṛ), this is the *lakṣmaṇa-mantra*. It is conjoined with the unsurpassed *sa* (Sa). Its seer (*ṛṣi*) is I myself, Mahādeva; its meter (*chandas*) is said to be Gāyatrī; Lakṣmaṇa is declared to be the deity (*devatā*); *Laṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and indeed, *Hi* is its power (*śakti*). "Namaḥ" is the application (*viniyoga*) for the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*). I worship on my arm the Lord of Mūrmilā, who has two arms, a body radiant like gold, eyes like lotuses, holding a bow and arrows, his mind intent on service to Rāma, and like Rāma himself, seated upon a golden throne. This worship is declared to be Vaiṣṇava, complete with limbs (*aṅga*) but devoid of further enclosures (*āvaraṇa*).

Having performed seven hundred thousand recitations (*puraścaryā*), one shall then achieve success; this was previously declared by the Goddess herself along with Rāma. This same procedure applies to Bharata and likewise to Śatrughna.

One who is devoted to the worship of Śrī Rāma shall always be victorious through this [practice]. Whether at the beginning or at the end of the worship of Rāghava, these [rites] must also be performed by those desiring the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation. Primarily, separately, or as auxiliary parts within the *Rāmapīṭha*, one should perform the worship of Hanumān as well without sloth, having first uttered the word "namas."

Then, one should place the word *Hanumate*, the word *Āñjaneya*, and likewise the word *Mahābala*, followed by the wife of Fire (Svāhā). This supreme mantra of Hanumān is said to grant all accomplishments (*siddhis*) and bestow success upon everyone;
it is known as the "Garland" (*Mālā*) mantra, the Wind-god’s mantra that grants all success. Lakṣmaṇa, however, should always be worshipped with preeminence at all times.

Having performed the entire network of Vaiṣṇava ritual placements (*nyāsa*) with a concentrated mind, and having duly performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and the placement of the Mother-letters (*mātṛkā*) with effort, one should perform the mental worship (*mānasī-pūjā*) and the external worship.

O Sage, if that person desires the fruitfulness of the worship of Śrī Rāma—whether performed by himself constantly at the three junctions of the day or at a single time—he should perform it with great detail according to those efforts. O Muni, there are indeed many varieties of the Śrī Rāma mantras; therefore, they should always and perpetually be practiced by the seekers of Saumitri (Lakṣmaṇa).

Just as the Supreme Brahman is to be served here in this world by those seeking liberation, so too should the mantra of Lakṣmaṇa be constantly served in this life. [This is for the sake of] the fruitfulness of the ten-syllable and other such mantras.

Even one who merely desires [liberation] should always serve this mantra, for it bestows both worldly and otherworldly fruits. Those who chant the Rāma-mantra without first chanting the Lakṣmaṇa-mantra do not attain the fruit of their recitation, even if they are highly skilled. Furthermore, no discrimination between enemy and friend should be made here; those devoted to the worship of Rāma should always and properly serve this [mantra]. Established in solitude, one should constantly employ the Lakṣmaṇa-mantra. One is liberated from all sins, even those accumulated through repeated actions of mind, speech, and body, and one attains all desired objects without exception.

One is liberated from multitudes of great sins in manifold ways; there is no doubt in this. One attains all desires and the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. (44) [Thus ends the thirtieth chapter of the Śrī Agastya Saṃhitā. (30) Agastya said: I shall now explain, according to my ability, the application of the mantra previously mentioned, along with its secret and in full detail. Indeed, for the sake of its application, this mantra was properly taught in the past by the Wielder of the Bow (Śārṅgin) to Arjuna; by means of this alone, Dhanañjaya conquered the quarters.
He subdued even many powerful enemies and established Dharmarāja in his supreme ancestral kingdom. This mantra, which grants victory, is the sole means for attaining sovereignty;

one who, with a concentrated mind, recites it one hundred thousand times, shall undoubtedly regain a lost kingdom in no time. Meditating single-mindedly on Rāma as consecrated in Ayodhyā, and having chanted this fifty thousand times, one shall recover a lost kingdom. Standing in solitude and reciting it ten thousand times while meditating on Him as liberated from the serpent-noose, one attains the same result.

Likewise, one shall be released from shackles and other such bonds; by meditating on the great medicine brought by Añjanī and removing all pain, a person conquers untimely death through ten million recitations (*jāpya*). By meditating with a concentrated mind upon him who took the life of Indrajit, one may swiftly conquer even a vast host of invincible enemies. By meditating on him whose mind was intent on cutting off the tip of his own nose, and performing a thousand recitations, one may conquer Indra and the other gods. Constantly remembering his eternal being for the sake of serving the lotus-feet of Rāma, one should perform recitation with that splendor in a solitary place, O Great One.

It destroys many diseases, such as consumption, epilepsy, and leprosy, at that very moment. Restraining the senses, one should recite [the mantra] seven thousand times daily for three months while maintaining a fixed diet; one should worship according to the rules with one hundred and eight flawless *śatapatra* flowers, and offer milk-rice mixed with sugar as an oblation (*naivedya*) according to the ritual, O Sage.

Having anointed oneself with sandalwood paste mixed with camphor, the best of the twice-born, having thus worshipped the God daily, shall be liberated from leprosy and other diseases that are difficult to cure.

Numerous varieties of skin diseases, such as *maṇḍala* and others, all go to destruction in an instant, even those that are difficult to treat. One who is strictly restricted in diet, has conquered the senses, and recites [the mantra] according to the prescribed rule for six months, is liberated from the disease of consumption (*kṣayaroga*). With a concentrated mind, one should recite the mantra while offering oblations of black gram cakes and food;

thus one is liberated in an instant, even from many types of wind-diseases (*vātaroga*). Having consecrated water three times daily with the mantra, one should drink it with devotion during the twilight hours.

One is liberated from all diseases; having destroyed poverty, one attains unsurpassed prosperity. There shall never be contact with the defects of poison and the like. By washing the face daily with devotion and a concentrated mind, one conquers even the most terrible diseases arising in the mouth, eyes, and other parts. Having drunk consecrated water, one conquers many diseases of the stomach. By making a gift of an image of the Lord with devotion according to the prescribed rite, one is liberated from all diseases; there is no doubt in this matter. [The same applies for] a daughter...

O ascetic, by meditating on him whose mind is intent on grasping the hand of Urvaśī, reciting his name one hundred thousand times, and having offered oblations with parched grain (*lāja*) according to the ten-part rule (*daśāṃsa*), one will quickly obtain the desired maiden.

One who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*), restrained in his vows, and focused on the mantras for the immobilization (*stambhana*) of women, should constantly remember [the deity] according to the rules for three months with undistracted mind. By performing worship first and reciting [the mantra] seven thousand times while controlling the senses, he will certainly become a knower of the reality (*tattva*) of all sciences (*vidyā*). Meditate upon Viśvāmitra, the best of sacrificers, whose prowess is wonderful in sacrifice.

By reciting [the mantra] ten million times, one is liberated from fears after a long time. The knower of mantras, having performed the twilight worship according to rule with the root mantra, being self-restrained at the three junctions of the day and having performed his daily rites, and having received initiation according to the prescribed method preceded by the permission of the guru, is liberated from all sins and goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. Even those who perform worship for worldly gains do not lead him away if he worships Hari without desire. Having obtained initiation according to the rule from a guru who is free from taint, devoted to his own conduct, and a householder who has conquered his senses—

One should perform the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) according to the rules by means of the essence of its knowledge; with a stainless mind, having burnt away all floods of merit and sin, one shall attain the eternal state from which there is no return.

Or, if one has desires, having enjoyed desired objects and delightful pleasures, and having lived for a long time as one who remembers past births, one goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. Just as the occurrence of sin does not exist for one who employs the mantras of Śrī Rāma, it is not so for the mantra of Lakṣmaṇa; rather, they attain the supreme goal. This mantra was formerly [revealed] by Brahmā.

With a mind free from theft, during a solar eclipse at Kurukṣetra, this mantra was indeed given to me with great reverence; and I too have worshipped it with a heart full of devotion. Having observed his devotion to the Guru, the Sage made me his very hand.

Many people in the world, having worshipped this mantra many times, attained their desired objects and went to the abode of Viṣṇu. A mantra equal to this has never been seen by me anywhere—whether among the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, Gāṇapatya, or Vāma mantras, O Muni. Some exist merely for the sake of satisfaction, while others are means for worldly ends.
"And this alone, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, reigns supreme. [Thus ends the thirty-first chapter of the Śrī Agastisaṃhitā.
(31) Sutīkṣṇa said: "O Sage, whose mind is resolved and who knows the essential truth of all the Vedas, I have been thoroughly instructed in many ways by you, a compassionate treasury of mercy.

Previously ignorant and likewise dull-witted, through your grace I have become possessed of knowledge and freed from all taint. My mind is now firmly attached to Rāma, the Supreme Brahman, O Lakṣmaṇa..."

"O Hanumān, O bull among sages, you have indeed said that there is no Veda whatsoever for those who have been cast out; yet, O best of munis, I desire to know the performance of the mantra of that Lord.
Since you are well-disposed toward me, O ocean of compassion, please explain it all. Agastya said: "O sage, I have been perfectly reminded by you, you who possess faith.

This *Āñjaneya-mantra*, the sole means for attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation in this world, was revealed by Śaṅkara desiring the welfare of the worlds—[a mantra] which [overcomes] ghosts, spirits, piśācas, and the like, as well as ḍākinīs and brahma-rākṣasas..."

Seeing him intent on the performance of mantras, they fled. The seer is Īśvara; the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh; Hanumān is declared the deity; *ha* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); the *antyaja*s (the final letters) are the power (*śakti*); *hā* three times is declared the pillar (*kīlaka*); and *hasau* is the Vedic invocation (*veda*). One should utter that *taṃ* syllable, which is a circle of light that whitens the third world with the canopy of its glory; it is the state of Vajradeha and likewise the state of the incarnation of Rudra. One should utter the supreme *laṃ*, the burner of the city of Laṅkā; it is the leaping across the ocean and the bringer of death to the Ten-necked one (*Rāvaṇa*). It is the state of consoling Sītā and the birth from the womb of Mañjanī; it is the delight of Śrī Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, the rampart for the monkey army, and the common ground for Sugrīva. It is the universal expulsion (*uccāṭana*) and the profound sound "O celibate youth! (*vāla-brahmacārin*).

Then one should utter the *pada* for the destruction of *ḍākinīs*, followed by the *Tāra* (*om*). Having pronounced the three *Māyā-hā*s (*hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ*), one should then sprinkle with ashes. Then one should recite twice: "Take away all poison, destroy power, crush fear, accomplish all tasks!"—*hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This mantra, known as the "Garland," grants all desires. The wise practitioner should then recite: "Salutation to the Blessed One, the Eye-ointment One" (*namo bhagavate cāñjaneyāya*) with the two thumbs; immediately after, "To the Form of Rudra" (*rudramūrtaye*) with the two index fingers; and likewise, "To the Purifier of Rāma" (*rāmapūtāya*) with the two little fingers.

This mantra has been proclaimed for the purpose of warding off the Brahmāstra weapon. O Sage, having thus performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one should meditate with undistracted mind upon [the deity] who resembles crystal, possesses the luster of gold, has two arms, and has joined his palms in reverence; whose lotus-face is repeatedly beautified by a pair of earrings. One should perform ten thousand recitations (*ayuta*) as the preliminary service (*puraścaryā*) before Rāma or Śiva, and likewise offer worship on either a Vaiṣṇava or Śaiva pedestal. Furthermore, eating only at night and with senses subdued, one should perform the recitation daily with repetitions for the sake of curing minor ailments, O Sage, numbering one hundred and eight times.

Furthermore, by reciting it for three days, one is liberated from the fear of elemental spirits (*bhūta*); by reciting it one hundred and eight times for the pacification of *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and the like, one certainly becomes free from that fear—of this there is no doubt.

For the sake of pacifying great diseases and other afflictions, one who maintains a restricted diet and recites it one thousand and eight times will surely be liberated from them. For kings desiring victory, there is no other [means] than this; one who maintains a restricted diet and is self-controlled should meditate on the Slayer of Rākṣasas. Being observant of the rules, he shall recite it and conquer even an invincible enemy through the power of concentration.

Even while remembering Yatu-sugrīva as the reconciler, one undoubtedly attains peace through ten thousand recitations. By meditating upon and chanting ten thousand times, one who has set fire to Laṅkā surely burns the enemy kingdom like a blazing fire, O sinless one. For the sake of victory over those lions among enemies, there is no other [deity] than this; whoever always worships Hanumān in their home, it is said that his prosperity shall be unshakable through his mantra. His life shall indeed be long, and he shall be victorious everywhere. [He shall be the destroyer of the hosts of beings...]

It arises simply by the grace of the Lord; thus has the sixfold sequence (*ṣaṭkrama*) of the Śaivas and Vaiṣṇavas been shown here. There is no other means than this mantra of Hanumān. For thieves, tigers, elephants, and the like, this alone is the ultimate refuge. For those whose kingdoms have been seized by others, or who are again oppressed by enemies, let the enemy army see a man clad in armor for battle. He who remembers Hanumān at the time of departure and goes forth from his own home with speed attains his desired goal. [He is] the protector during sleep...
